title: Marseilles—The Arrival
summary: On 24 February 1815 the ship Pharaon sails into Marseilles under its young mate, Edmond Dantès, whose captain died at sea. The owner, M. Morrel, promises to make him captain, and the supercargo Danglars watches him with jealous hatred.
details: The three-masted merchant ship Pharaon arrives at Marseilles, steered in by a capable nineteen-year-old mate, Edmond Dantès. The shipowner, M. Morrel, rows out to meet her and learns that Captain Leclere died of brain fever on the voyage. The cargo is safe, and Dantès took command himself.

Danglars, the ship's supercargo (the officer in charge of the cargo and accounts), is about twenty-six. He fawns on his bosses, bullies those below him, and the crew dislikes him as much as they love Dantès. He tries to turn Morrel against Dantès, complaining that Dantès lost a day and a half by stopping at the island of Elba. Dantès explains that the dying captain asked him to carry a packet to Marshal Bertrand there. While on Elba he even spoke with the exiled emperor Napoleon, who remembered Morrel's uncle Policar. Morrel quietly approves, but warns that the visit could cause trouble if it became known. Danglars also hints that Leclere gave Dantès a letter, which shows he was eavesdropping at the captain's door.

Morrel invites Dantès to dinner, but Dantès turns him down: he wants to see his father first, and then his fiancée, Mercédès, at the Catalan village. He asks for leave to get married and then travel to Paris. Morrel says he means to make him captain, if he can win over his partner. Asked about Danglars, Dantès admits they quarrelled once (he even proposed settling it on the island of Monte Cristo) but praises his work. As Dantès goes ashore, Morrel and Danglars both watch him leave, with very different expressions.

title: Father and Son
summary: Dantès finds his elderly father half-starved: the old man paid off Edmond's debt to their neighbour Caderousse and lived on almost nothing. The envious Caderousse visits, then reports to Danglars, and the two go off to spy on Dantès and Mercédès.
details: Dantès hurries to his father's small upstairs room in Marseilles. The old man nearly faints for joy. Edmond soon learns that the cupboards are empty. Their neighbour Caderousse demanded repayment of a 140-franc debt Edmond owed him, so his father paid it out of the 200 francs Edmond had left him and lived on sixty francs for three months. Edmond empties his pockets onto the table and promises his father a better life once he is captain.

Caderousse, a tailor of about twenty-five, comes to congratulate Edmond. His friendly words cover envy, and he eyes the money greedily. He teases Edmond for refusing Morrel's dinner invitation and needles him about Mercédès having plenty of admirers. Dantès answers calmly that she will stay faithful, and leaves for the Catalan village.

Outside, Caderousse meets Danglars, who has been waiting for him. He complains that Dantès is 'insolent' about his promotion, and Danglars mutters that if they choose, Dantès may end up even lower than he is now. Caderousse mentions that Mercédès is always seen with a tall, fierce young Catalan she calls her cousin. Sensing a useful rival, Danglars takes Caderousse to La Réserve, an inn near the Catalan village, to drink and watch what happens.

title: The Catalans
summary: In the Catalan village, Mercédès firmly refuses her cousin Fernand, who loves her. Dantès arrives and she forces the two men to shake hands. Fernand runs off and is drawn into drinking with Danglars and Caderousse, and Danglars begins to see a way to ruin Dantès.
details: The Catalans are a close-knit community of Spanish origin living on a point of land outside Marseilles. There, the beautiful young Mercédès turns down yet another proposal from her cousin Fernand, a fisherman. She is a poor orphan and loves him only as a brother, because her heart belongs to Edmond Dantès. When Fernand hints that the sailor may be faithless or dead, she says that if Edmond dies, she will die too.

At that moment Edmond calls from outside and the lovers embrace. Dantès sees Fernand's threatening face, and Fernand's hand goes to his knife. Mercédès says that if any harm comes to Edmond she will throw herself from a cliff, and with a commanding look she makes Fernand shake Edmond's hand. Fernand then rushes out in despair.

Caderousse and Danglars call him into their arbour at the inn. The drunken Caderousse mocks him as a rejected lover while Danglars watches closely. When the happy couple pass by, Dantès announces that the wedding feast will be the next day or the day after, and invites them all, Fernand included. He adds that he must go to Paris afterwards to carry out Captain Leclere's last commission. Danglars realises this means the letter from Elba, and an idea forms in his mind.

title: Conspiracy
summary: Danglars eggs Fernand on, then writes an anonymous letter with his left hand denouncing Dantès as a Bonapartist agent. He pretends it is a joke and throws it away, but Fernand secretly picks it up.
details: Danglars works on Fernand, who admits he would kill Dantès except that Mercédès has sworn to die if Edmond does. Danglars suggests there is no need for murder: prison walls separate lovers as well as a tombstone. The very drunk Caderousse keeps protesting that Dantès is his friend and must not be harmed, so Danglars keeps refilling his glass.

Calling for pen, ink and paper, Danglars points out that Dantès stopped at Elba, where Napoleon was in exile. He writes a denunciation with his left hand so the handwriting cannot be traced, addressed to the king's attorney (the royal prosecutor). It claims that Dantès carried a letter from Murat to 'the usurper' Napoleon, and from Napoleon to the Bonapartist committee in Paris, and that proof will be found on him, at his father's, or in his cabin.

Caderousse, grasping what this means, calls it an infamous shame. Danglars crumples the paper and tosses it into a corner of the arbour, saying it was only a joke. As Danglars leads the staggering Caderousse home, he looks back and sees Fernand pick up the letter, pocket it, and hurry towards the city. Satisfied, Danglars tells himself that the plan will now work on its own.

title: The Marriage Feast
summary: At the joyful feast, Dantès announces that he and Mercédès will marry that very afternoon. Before they can leave, soldiers arrive and arrest him. Morrel returns with the news that the charge is Bonapartist conspiracy, and Danglars frightens Caderousse into silence.
details: The feast is held at La Réserve. Morrel himself attends, which the crew takes as proof that Dantès will be captain. Old Dantès is dressed in his finest. Mercédès seats Fernand beside her as a 'brother', which torments him. Dantès announces that, thanks to Morrel's help, the mayor will marry them at half past two that very day. He will then go to Paris and hold a second celebration on his return.

As the party sets off, a magistrate arrives with soldiers and arrests Dantès 'in the name of the law', giving no reason. Dantès calmly says it must be a mistake and is driven away while Mercédès cries out to him. Fernand slips out and returns pale. Caderousse now remembers the letter and accuses Danglars, who insists he threw it away and blames Fernand. To explain the arrest, Danglars suggests some smuggled goods were found aboard.

Morrel comes back looking grave: Dantès is charged with being a Bonapartist agent. Caderousse wants to confess, but Danglars warns him that anyone who defends Dantès may be treated as his accomplice, and selfish fear wins. Fernand takes Mercédès home. Morrel then hands Danglars temporary command of the Pharaon and goes to plead with M. de Villefort, the deputy prosecutor. Danglars privately rejoices.

title: The Deputy Procureur du Roi
summary: At the same hour, the deputy procureur du roi (the king's deputy prosecutor), Villefort, is celebrating his own betrothal to Renée de Saint-Méran among fierce royalists. We learn his father is the Bonapartist Noirtier. He is called away to deal with the denunciation of Dantès.
details: In an aristocratic mansion in Marseilles, a very different engagement party is under way. The guests are royalists who loathe Napoleon, now exiled on Elba. The Marquis de Saint-Méran toasts King Louis XVIII. His stern wife, the marquise, reminds her future son-in-law, M. de Villefort, that his father was a Girondin (a moderate revolutionary) named Noirtier who later served Napoleon as a senator.

Villefort explains that he has disowned his father's politics and even his name: Noirtier is a Bonapartist, while he is a loyal royalist called de Villefort. The marquise reminds him that the family has vouched for his loyalty to the king, so he must be especially hard on any conspirator. Villefort boasts about the death sentences he has won in court. His gentle fiancée, Renée, is frightened and begs him to be merciful to those she pleads for. The Comte de Salvieux reports that the king himself praised Villefort and approved the match.

A servant calls Villefort out. He returns delighted and reads the anonymous letter accusing Edmond Dantès, which his office opened in the chief prosecutor's absence; the accused is already held at his house. Renée begs him to show mercy on the day of their betrothal. He promises to be lenient if he can, then leaves happily to do his duty.

title: The Examination
summary: Villefort questions Dantès, is convinced he is innocent, and is ready to free him, until he sees that the letter from Elba is addressed to his own father, Noirtier. He burns it and, while pretending to protect Dantès, secretly decides to keep him locked up.
details: Gérard de Villefort, twenty-seven, rich and about to make an advantageous marriage, walks to his office. On the way Morrel begs him to free Dantès, but Villefort, a royalist, treats the shipowner coldly as a suspected Bonapartist.

Dantès is calm and open. He says he is nineteen, has no politics, and loves only his father, Morrel and Mercédès. He does not recognise the handwriting of the denunciation. He explains how the dying Captain Leclere ordered him to take a packet and a ring to the grand-marshal on Elba, who gave him a letter for someone in Paris. Villefort believes him, thinks of pleasing Renée, and tells him he may go once he hands over the letter.

Then he learns the address: M. Noirtier, Rue Coq-Héron, Paris. Villefort turns white and reads the letter three times, fearing that if its contents come out, his connection to Noirtier will ruin him. He asks whether Dantès has shown it to anyone, burns it in the fire, and makes Dantès swear never to mention the letter or the name. Dantès thanks him as a friend. Villefort quietly gives an order to a police agent, then sinks into a chair. He curses his father's past, then smiles: this letter, which could have ruined him, will make his fortune.

title: The Château d’If
summary: Instead of being released, Dantès is taken by boat at night to the Château d'If, a grim island fortress for political prisoners. He begs to see the governor and threatens a jailer, so he is thrown into an underground dungeon.
details: Dantès is held in a cell in the Palais de Justice until about ten at night, still trusting Villefort's promise. Gendarmes then take him by carriage to the harbour and row him out to sea. He passes La Réserve, where the party continues without him, and the Catalan village, where a single light burns in Mercédès' window. Pride stops him from shouting to her.

When a gendarme finally tells him they are going to the Château d'If, Dantès is horrified: there has been no trial and no formalities. He tries to leap overboard but is pinned down at gunpoint. He is locked in a damp cell for the night.

Over the next days he refuses to eat and keeps demanding to see the governor. He bitterly regrets that he did not swim for freedom during the boat trip; he is a famous swimmer and speaks Italian and Spanish. The jailer warns that a former prisoner of the cell, an abbé who kept offering the governor a million francs for his freedom, went mad and was moved to a dungeon. Dantès offers the jailer a hundred crowns to carry a message to Mercédès. When he is refused, he threatens the jailer with a stool. Labelled a madman, he is marched down fifteen steps into a dark dungeon, already close to losing his mind.

title: The Evening of the Betrothal
summary: Villefort rushes to Paris to warn the king of a Napoleonic plot and win the credit himself. He brushes off a pleading Mercédès and feels the first stab of lasting remorse. We see how each of Dantès' friends and enemies spends the night.
details: Back at the Saint-Méran house, Villefort privately tells the marquis that urgent business calls him to Paris. He advises him to sell all his government bonds at once, a hint that he expects political upheaval. He also asks for a letter from the Comte de Salvieux that will get him straight into the king's presence. He refuses to go through the keeper of the seals, because he wants all the credit for his discovery.

At his door he finds Mercédès, who has come to ask about Edmond. Villefort tells her coldly that Dantès is a great criminal and is no longer in his hands. Alone, he is seized by remorse: he has destroyed an innocent man to protect his own ambition. Had Renée or Mercédès pleaded at that moment, he might have signed the release. But only his valet comes in, to announce the carriage, and Villefort leaves. Renée, far from pleading for Dantès, now resents the prisoner whose 'crime' has taken her fiancé away.

Mercédès spends the night in despair with Fernand kneeling at her side. Morrel's appeals to influential friends are refused, since Dantès is now branded a Bonapartist. Caderousse shuts himself in with brandy but cannot drown his conscience. Only Danglars is content, sure of his place on the Pharaon, and he sleeps soundly. Old Dantès waits in agony for news.

title: The King’s Closet at the Tuileries
summary: In Paris, King Louis XVIII teases his anxious adviser Blacas and trusts his complacent police minister. Then Villefort arrives and warns that Napoleon is preparing to leave Elba.
details: In his private study at the Tuileries palace, Louis XVIII annotates his Horace while the Duc de Blacas warns of a storm brewing in the south. The king jokes away his fears. The minister of police, Baron Dandré, reports that Napoleon is bored and possibly going mad on Elba, even telling his old soldiers to 'serve the good king'.

Blacas says that a messenger recommended by M. de Salvieux has raced from Marseilles with alarming news. When the king hears the name Villefort, he grows serious. He knows Villefort's father is Noirtier, the former Girondin and senator, but says the son is so ambitious that he would sacrifice even his father.

Villefort, still dusty from the road, is shown in. He tells the king that Napoleon is arming ships and may already have left Elba, perhaps to land in Italy or France. He claims to have learned this from a Bonapartist sailor he arrested, whom he describes as carrying a spoken message for a Paris Bonapartist whose name he 'could not extract'. He says nothing about the letter or its address. Louis XVIII is confident the coast is well guarded, but promises his gratitude. Just then the minister of police reappears at the door, pale and trembling.

title: The Corsican Ogre
summary: News arrives that Napoleon has landed in France. The king rewards Villefort with the Legion of Honour, but Villefort is shaken when the suspect in a general's murder sounds like his father, and then that very man turns up at his hotel.
details: Dandré confesses that Napoleon left Elba on 26 February and landed near Antibes on 1 March, and that he is advancing by way of Gap and Sisteron. The king learns this only on 3 March, by telegraph, and is furious and humiliated. He contrasts his whole police force with the single magistrate who foresaw it. Villefort shrewdly defends the minister, earning his gratitude, partly because a desperate minister might question Dantès and uncover the truth.

The king then asks about the death of General Quesnel, a royalist who disappeared after being lured to a Bonapartist club in the Rue Saint-Jacques. The police now think he was murdered, not a suicide. They describe the suspect: about fifty, dark, with black whiskers, a blue frock-coat buttoned to the chin and the rosette of the Legion of Honour, last seen near the Rue Coq-Héron. Villefort nearly collapses, then breathes again when he hears the man escaped.

The king pointedly asks whether he has visited his father, then gives him his own Legion of Honour cross. Back at his hotel, Villefort is told that a stranger matching the police description is asking for him. The visitor walks in and greets him as 'my dear Gérard'. It is his father.

title: Father and Son
summary: Noirtier, a leading Bonapartist, calmly admits his role in the club linked to General Quesnel's death and predicts Napoleon will reach Paris within weeks. He shaves off his whiskers to disguise himself and walks out past the police.
details: Noirtier locks the doors and teases his son for being in Paris instead of at his wedding. Villefort says he came to save him. Noirtier coolly confirms that he is vice-president of the Bonapartist club at No. 53 Rue Saint-Jacques. Villefort explains that he intercepted a letter from Elba addressed to Noirtier and burned it, because it would have got his father shot and ruined his own career.

Noirtier gives his own account of General Quesnel. The club believed he was on their side and told him the whole plan for Napoleon's return. Quesnel said he was a royalist, swore an oath of silence, was 'allowed to depart free', and 'lost his way'. Noirtier insists that in politics there are no murders, only obstacles removed. He predicts that Napoleon will be at Grenoble, then Lyons, and in Paris by around the 20th, welcomed rather than resisted, and proves how good his own network is by having found his son within half an hour of his arrival.

When Villefort repeats the police description, Noirtier shaves off his black whiskers and puts on his son's brown coat and hat. He tells Gérard to go home quietly and keep his head down, promising to protect him in return. He strolls past the agents watching the street. Villefort hides his father's clothes, burns the cane, and hurries back to Marseilles, hearing on the way that Napoleon has entered Grenoble.

title: The Hundred Days
summary: During Napoleon's brief return to power, Villefort tricks Morrel into writing a petition that makes Dantès look like a dangerous Bonapartist, and keeps it. After Waterloo, Dantès is forgotten in prison, his enemies move on, and his father dies.
details: Napoleon retakes the throne. Noirtier's influence protects Villefort's post, and Villefort postpones his marriage until he sees which side will win. With Bonapartists now in favour, Morrel asks what has become of Dantès. Villefort coolly pretends to look him up in the register, claims he was sent off to some distant fortress, and explains that some prisoners are made to vanish without records. He then 'helps' Morrel write a petition to the minister. It praises Dantès as one of the most active agents of Napoleon's return, and Villefort certifies it.

Instead of sending it, Villefort keeps the petition, which would be damning if the king returned. After Waterloo, Louis XVIII is restored. Villefort becomes king's prosecutor at Toulouse and marries Renée de Saint-Méran. Dantès stays in his dungeon, forgotten by everyone.

Danglars, afraid Dantès might return for revenge, gets a recommendation from Morrel and goes to Madrid to work for a Spanish merchant, and nothing more is heard of him. Fernand broods over plans to kill Dantès and himself, then is called up in Napoleon's last conscription. Mercédès, grateful for his kindness, sends him off calling him her brother, which gives him hope. Caderousse, married and older, is sent to the frontier. Old Dantès loses all hope when Napoleon falls and dies in Mercédès' arms five months after his son's arrest. Morrel bravely pays for the funeral, even though helping a 'Bonapartist's' father is dangerous.

title: The Two Prisoners
summary: In July 1816 a prison inspector visits the dungeons. Dantès humbly begs for a trial, and the inspector promises to look into it. In another cell, the 'mad' Abbé Faria offers millions for his freedom. A note in Dantès' file dooms his hopes.
details: A year after the king's return, an inspector-general of prisons tours the Château d'If with the governor. He is shown the 'dangerous' prisoner who once attacked the turnkey Antoine. Dantès, now subdued, asks only to know his crime and be tried. He was arrested on 28 February 1815, and it is now 30 July 1816: seventeen months, which to him feel like seventeen ages. He names Villefort as the man who arrested him and calls him kind. Moved, the inspector promises to examine his case.

Next they visit No. 27, the Abbé Faria, an Italian priest imprisoned since 1811 and thought to have gone mad in 1813. He is found drawing geometry on the floor of his cell. Faria says he was secretary to Cardinal Spada for twenty years and was arrested at Piombino. He dreamed of a united Italy. He asks to speak privately about a huge treasure and offers five, then six, millions for his liberty, promising to stay in prison while they check. The officials laugh it off as the familiar madness.

The inspector finds a note in Dantès' file, written in a different hand and added after he was locked up: 'Violent Bonapartist; took an active part in the return from Elba.' It echoes the petition Villefort kept. The inspector writes 'Nothing to be done.' Dantès, newly hopeful, starts marking the days on the wall, but months pass with no change. A new governor arrives who knows prisoners only by number, and Dantès becomes simply 'number 34'.

title: Number 34 and Number 27
summary: After years of despair, Dantès tries to starve himself to death, until he hears someone digging behind his wall. He starts tunnelling towards the sound, and finally the other prisoner, No. 27, breaks through into his cell.
details: Dantès goes through every stage of a prisoner's suffering: pride, doubt, pleading, prayer, then rage against the unknown enemies who wrote the letter. He finally decides to die by starving himself, secretly throwing his food out of the window. Nearly four years in, close to death, he hears a scraping sound inside the wall.

Hope returns. Dantès eats again, knocks to test whether the noise is a workman or a prisoner, and concludes from the cautious silence that it is a fellow captive. With a shard of a broken jug and then the iron handle of the soup saucepan, which he tricks the jailer into leaving, he digs out a stone. He reflects that he has wasted six years in prison when he could have been working like this.

When a beam blocks his way and he cries out to God in despair, a voice answers from below. The stranger has been in prison since 1811 and has never heard of Napoleon's fall. He explains that he was digging towards the sea but miscalculated and reached the wrong wall. He gives his name only as 'No. 27' and is wary, but is reassured by Dantès' age and sincerity. Dantès, who was nineteen at his arrest and is now not quite twenty-six, begs not to be abandoned, offering to love him like a father. The next day the floor gives way and an old man climbs up into his cell.

title: A Learned Italian
summary: The newcomer is the Abbé Faria, a brilliant Italian scholar. He has made his own tools, pens, ink and paper, and has written a whole book in prison. His escape plan has failed, but his determination inspires Dantès to suggest a new one.
details: The stranger is small, about sixty, with white hair and a long black beard. He shows Dantès a chisel made from a bed clamp, which he used to dig the fifty-foot tunnel. Climbing onto Dantès' shoulders, he sees that the window looks onto a gallery patrolled by soldiers, so escape through this cell is impossible. He introduces himself as the Abbé Faria, imprisoned since 1811. He was jailed for dreaming of uniting Italy and was betrayed by a ruler he trusted. He admits he is the 'mad priest' of the Château d'If.

Faria accepts the failure as God's will, but his example fires Dantès with fresh courage: if this old man could do so much, a young, strong swimmer could do more. Dantès proposes cutting a side tunnel into the gallery and killing the sentry. Faria refuses to shed blood. He prefers to wait patiently for a lucky chance, as in history's famous escapes.

Dantès is amazed to learn what Faria has done alone in his cell. He has written a treatise on a united Italian monarchy on strips of linen made smooth by a chemical process. He makes pens from fish cartilage and ink from soot and wine, and writes in his own blood for important notes. He knows some 150 books by heart and speaks five modern languages. Eager to see it all, Dantès follows him into the tunnel.

title: The Abbé’s Chamber
summary: Faria shows Dantès that Danglars and Fernand denounced him and that Villefort buried him to protect his father, Noirtier. Dantès swears revenge. Faria educates him, and they dig an escape tunnel until a fit leaves Faria paralysed.
details: In his own cell Faria tells the time by the sun, and shows his linen manuscript, his fish-bone pens, his knives, a lamp made from melted fat, and a rope ladder. Dantès tells his story. Faria applies a simple rule: look for whoever gains from the crime. Danglars wanted the captaincy, overheard Captain Leclere and saw the letter. Fernand wanted Mercédès. Dantès remembers seeing them with Caderousse and pen, ink and paper at the inn the day before his wedding. Faria writes with his left hand to show how the accusation's handwriting was disguised.

Then Faria questions him about the deputy prosecutor who burned the letter. Hearing the names Noirtier and Villefort, he laughs and explains that Noirtier was Villefort's father. Stunned, Dantès goes back to his cell and swears a solemn oath of vengeance. Faria regrets having planted that passion in him.

Dantès asks to be taught, and Faria teaches him mathematics, history, science and languages. Within a year Dantès is a new man, cultivated and polished. Faria finally agrees to an escape plan as long as the sentry is harmed only as a last resort. For fifteen months they tunnel beneath the gallery.

On the eve of escape, Faria is struck by a seizure. Following his instructions, Dantès gives him drops of a red remedy, and he revives. But his right arm and leg are paralysed. He warns that a third attack, like the ones that killed his father and grandfather, will kill him. He urges Dantès to flee alone, but Dantès swears never to leave him while he lives.

title: The Treasure
summary: Faria reveals his secret: a half-burnt letter from 1498 in which Cardinal Spada describes a vast treasure hidden in the caves of the island of Monte Cristo. Faria names Dantès as his heir and calls him his son.
details: Faria shows Dantès a scorched paper and says it is his treasure, half of which now belongs to Dantès. Dantès fears the illness has made Faria truly mad and avoids him. That evening the paralysed abbé drags himself through the tunnel to tell his story.

Faria served the last Count of Spada, a descendant of a noble Roman family once said to be fabulously rich. In 1498, Pope Alexander VI and his son Cæsar Borgia made Cardinal Cæsar Spada and Cardinal Rospigliosi buy their posts, then invited them to dinner and poisoned them in order to seize their wealth. But Spada's fortune was never found. His will left his nephew only his papers and his gold-cornered breviary (prayer book). For three centuries the family searched in vain.

When the last count died, he left Faria his library and the breviary. In 1807, lighting a candle with an old bookmark from the breviary, Faria saw writing appear in the heat: invisible ink. With a second fragment he reconstructed the message. Spada had buried all his gold, jewels and gems, nearly two million Roman crowns, in the caves of the little island of Monte Cristo, to be found by raising the twentieth rock from a small creek to the east, in the furthest corner of the second opening. Faria was arrested as he set out to find it. The family is now extinct, so the treasure is his to give. Dantès protests that he is no relation, but Faria declares him 'the child of my captivity', and Dantès weeps on his neck.

title: The Third Attack
summary: Their tunnel is blocked when the gallery is rebuilt, and Faria prepares Dantès to recover the treasure alone. One night the third attack comes. Despite the remedy, Faria dies, and Dantès overhears the jailers planning to dispose of the body that evening.
details: Faria talks constantly of the good the fortune could do. Dantès, remembering his oath, thinks instead of the harm it could do to his enemies. Dantès knows Monte Cristo, a deserted, cone-shaped rock between Corsica and Elba, and draws a map for Faria. Then the ruined sea gallery is rebuilt and their escape route is sealed. Dantès tells Faria that his real treasure is their friendship and all the knowledge Faria has given him. Faria makes him learn Spada's letter by heart, destroys the second fragment, and coaches him on how to reach the island and search it.

One night Dantès wakes to hear Faria calling. The old man is seized by the fatal attack. He stops Dantès from calling for help, so that their secret will not be discovered, blesses him as his son, and tells him to hurry to Monte Cristo. His last words are 'Monte Cristo, forget not Monte Cristo!' Dantès gives him twelve drops, then the rest of the phial, but by dawn Faria is dead.

Hidden in the tunnel, Dantès hears the jailers mock 'the madman' and his treasure. The doctor confirms the death with a hot iron to the heel. The jailer recalls that Faria once cured his wife's illness. The governor orders the body sewn into a sack, without a mass, since the chaplain is away, and removed between ten and eleven that night. When the cell is empty, Dantès climbs out into it.

title: The Cemetery of the Château d’If
summary: Dantès takes his dead friend's place in the burial sack, planning to escape from the grave. Instead, the jailers tie a cannonball to his feet and fling him off the cliffs into the sea.
details: Sitting beside the sack that holds Faria's body, Dantès is tempted by suicide, then passes from despair to a fierce will to live, punish his enemies, and reward any friends. A thought strikes him: only the dead leave this place freely, so he will take the dead man's place.

Using Faria's homemade knife, he opens the sack and carries the body through the tunnel to his own bed, arranging it to look as if he is asleep with his face to the wall. He takes Faria's needle and thread, climbs into the sack naked and sews it shut from inside. He plans to slit the sack and fight his way out if he is discovered, or to dig himself out of the grave once the gravediggers leave.

The jailer's seven o'clock visit passes without trouble. Late that night two men carry the sack out into the windy night, joking that the old man is heavy. They stop, tie something heavy to his feet with a cord, and carry him up some steps while the waves crash below, joking that it is no night for a swim. They swing him, 'One! two! three!', and throw him into the air. Weighted with a thirty-six-pound cannonball, Dantès plunges into the icy sea. The sea, it turns out, is the cemetery of the Château d'If.

title: The Island of Tiboulen
summary: Dantès cuts himself free, swims through a storm to a barren islet, and is rescued by Genoese smugglers, posing as a shipwrecked Maltese sailor. It is 28 February 1829, fourteen years to the day since his arrest, and he renews his vow of revenge.
details: With the knife in his hand, Dantès slashes open the sack, cuts the cord holding the cannonball, and surfaces, diving again to avoid the torch-bearing gravediggers above. Steering by the Planier lighthouse, he swims for over an hour through rough sea and reaches the rocky islet of Tiboulen, where he collapses asleep. A violent storm breaks. By lightning he sees a fishing boat smash on the rocks and its crew drown.

At dawn, knowing the alarm will soon be raised at the fortress, he spots a Genoese tartan (a small Mediterranean sailing vessel) leaving Marseilles. He guesses its crew are smugglers. He puts on a drowned sailor's red cap, grabs a piece of wreckage and swims to cut across the boat's course. He is close to drowning when a sailor hauls him aboard by the hair.

He claims to be a Maltese sailor from last night's wreck. He explains his long hair and beard as a religious vow, then proves his skill by steering the boat flawlessly. The captain agrees to take him on. Jacopo, the sailor who saved him, lends him clothes. When the alarm gun fires from the Château d'If, Dantès calmly says a prisoner must have escaped and goes on sipping his rum. Jacopo tells him the date: 28 February 1829. Arrested at nineteen, Dantès is now thirty-three. He wonders what has become of Mercédès, and renews his oath of vengeance against Danglars, Fernand and Villefort as the tartan races towards Leghorn (Livorno).

title: The Smugglers
summary: Dantès sails with the smugglers of La Jeune Amélie, sees his transformed face in a mirror, is wounded in a skirmish with customs officers, and teaches the loyal Jacopo navigation. At last the smugglers choose Monte Cristo as a meeting place for their next job.
details: The master of La Jeune Amélie, a Genoese smuggler, comes to trust his skilled and tight-lipped recruit, though he never learns who Dantès really is. At Leghorn, Dantès has his hair and beard cut and sees himself for the first time in fourteen years. His open, smiling young face has become pale, stern and thoughtful, with eyes that can see in the dark and a changeable voice. No one who once knew him could recognise him. He signs on for three months only.

They run contraband to Corsica and Sardinia. On one run he passes close to Monte Cristo but has no chance to land. In a fight with customs men off the coast of Lucca, a customs officer is killed and Dantès is shot in the shoulder. He bears it calmly, and notices that the officer's death barely moves him: his heart is hardening. Jacopo, a Corsican, nurses him devotedly and indignantly refuses a share of his money, so Dantès grows fond of him and teaches him navigation and the stars, just as Faria once taught him.

After two and a half months Dantès has learned the smugglers' trade, their contacts and their secret signs, and has saved a hundred piastres. He plans to hire a boat of his own, but cannot find a way to search the island without companions. Then, at a smugglers' tavern in Leghorn, the master proposes the deserted island of Monte Cristo as a neutral place to exchange a valuable cargo. Dantès hides his joy and agrees they should sail the next night.

title: The Island of Monte Cristo
summary: On Monte Cristo, Dantès secretly finds carved marks on the rocks, then fakes a bad fall so the smugglers will leave him behind with a gun and a pickaxe. As soon as they sail out of sight, he springs up and heads for the treasure.
details: After a feverish night of dreams about jewelled caves, Dantès steers La Jeune Amélie to Monte Cristo. The crew call him 'the Maltese' and obey him almost like a commander, and the old master sees him as his natural successor. He is the first to leap ashore. He is shaken when Jacopo says there are no caves on the island, but decides the entrances must have been blocked up.

The next day, pretending to hunt wild goats, he sends Jacopo back with a kid for the cooks. Exploring alone, he finds marks carved by human hands on the rocks. They lead to a large round boulder, then seem to stop. Looking down at his comrades, he reflects that they will happily risk their lives for a few piastres, while he hopes for far more.

Running back when they signal that the meal is ready, he slips and falls down a slope. He claims to be in agony with a hurt knee and, the master suspects, broken ribs, and refuses to be moved. The master, Captain Baldi, must sail to deliver his cargo. Jacopo offers to give up his share and stay to nurse him, but Dantès insists on being left alone with biscuits, a gun, powder and a pickaxe, asking them to send a fishing boat or come back for him in a week.

He watches the tartan sail away, marvelling that he has found true friendship among such men. Once it is out of sight, Dantès leaps up as nimbly as a goat, takes his gun and pickaxe, and hurries to the rock where the marks ended, crying, like the fisherman in Faria's Arabian tale, 'Open Sesame!'

title: The Secret Cave
summary: Alone on Monte Cristo, Dantès follows Faria’s clues, blasts away a great rock, and makes his way through two hidden grottoes to Cardinal Spada’s chest, overflowing with gold coins, gold bars, and jewels.
details: Left behind by the smugglers after pretending to be injured, Dantès first climbs to the island’s highest point to make sure their ships have gone. He works out that the notches cut in the rocks lead to a hidden creek where Cardinal Spada could have landed in secret. A huge boulder puzzles him until he realizes it was never lifted into place: it was slid down a slope and wedged. Using the gunpowder his friend Jacopo left him, he blows out the wedge, levers the rock into the sea, and finds a flagstone with an iron ring, covering steps that lead underground.

Bracing himself for disappointment, he imagines that Cesare Borgia got there first, but goes down anyway with a wry “Perhaps!” The first grotto, lit through cracks in the rock, is empty. Remembering the words of the will, “in the farthest angle of the second opening,” he taps the walls, finds a patch of stucco painted to look like granite, and, after a moment when doubt nearly makes him faint, breaks through into a second, darker cave.

Digging in its corner, he strikes an oak chest bound with steel and engraved with the Spada coat of arms that Faria had so often drawn for him. He forces it open: one compartment holds gold coins, one bars of gold, one diamonds, pearls, and rubies. Half mad with joy, he runs wildly about the rocks, then kneels and prays. He counts a thousand gold ingots, twenty-five thousand old crowns, and handfuls of gems, then sleeps across the mouth of the cave with his gun beside him, a night of joy and terror.

title: The Unknown
summary: Dantès hides the treasure, sells a few gems, buys a yacht, and learns that his father is dead and Mercédès has vanished. Using the name Lord Wilmore, he returns unrecognized to Marseilles, buys his father’s old house, and visits the Catalans.
details: Dantès carefully disguises the cave entrance and, when the smugglers return six days later, pretends he is still lame. At Leghorn (Livorno) he sells four small diamonds to a dealer, then gives Jacopo a brand-new boat and money, explaining that he has just inherited a fortune from an uncle. He sends Jacopo to Marseilles to find out what has become of an old man named Louis Dantès and a young Catalan woman named Mercédès.

At Genoa, Dantès buys a fast little yacht that had been built for an Englishman, paying well over its price, and has the builder fit a secret three-part closet at the head of his bed. He sails alone to Monte Cristo, moves the whole treasure into the hidden closet, and spends a week learning how the boat handles. When Jacopo arrives, the news is grim: old Dantès is dead, and Mercédès has disappeared.

Confident that his face has changed beyond recognition, Dantès sails boldly into Marseilles on an English passport. A sailor from his old ship, the Pharaon, talks with him without recognizing him and is rewarded handsomely for his honesty. Dantès visits his father’s old rooms, now rented by a newly married couple, and weeps where the old man died. He learns that Caderousse, the former tailor downstairs, now keeps an inn near Beaucaire. Under the name on his passport, Lord Wilmore, he buys the house for far more than it is worth, spends an hour in the Catalan village asking about people long dead or gone, gives the family he questioned a new fishing boat, and rides out of Marseilles.

title: The Pont du Gard Inn
summary: Caderousse, now a struggling innkeeper with a sickly wife, is visited by an Italian priest who says Dantès died in prison and left a diamond to be shared among his friends. Caderousse reveals that old Dantès starved to death.
details: Caderousse and his wife, Madeleine, nicknamed La Carconte, keep a failing roadside inn between Beaucaire and Bellegarde; a new canal has carried off their trade. She is pale, shaking with marsh fever, and constantly complaining; he answers that it is God’s will. One scorching noon a priest arrives on horseback, speaking with a strong Italian accent. He studies Caderousse closely and makes sure he is the former tailor of the Allées de Meilhan in Marseilles.

The abbé asks about a young sailor named Dantès. Caderousse claims to have been his close friend and seems genuinely upset to hear that he died a broken man in prison. The abbé explains that a rich fellow prisoner gave Dantès a diamond worth fifty thousand francs, and that Dantès asked for it to be sold and shared among his father, his fiancée Mercédès, and three friends: Caderousse, Danglars, and Fernand. Asked how old Dantès died, Caderousse says the doctors called it a stomach illness, but the truth is he starved. The abbé leaps up, badly shaken.

La Carconte, listening from the stairs, warns her husband to keep quiet, because Fernand and Danglars are now rich and powerful. Caderousse hints that the two were traitors, not friends. When the abbé calmly says he will simply find them and give them their shares, greed wins: Caderousse bolts the door and sits down to tell the whole story, while the priest places himself in the shadows to listen.

title: The Story
summary: Caderousse tells the abbé everything: old Dantès’s slow death, the denunciation written by Danglars and posted by Fernand, Morrel’s near ruin, and how Danglars became a rich baron and Fernand the Count de Morcerf, husband of Mercédès. The abbé gives him the diamond.
details: Once promised secrecy, Caderousse describes old Dantès’s last months: pacing all night, refusing to leave home in case Edmond came back, quietly selling his belongings, and finally, using a doctor’s diet as an excuse, refusing all food until he died nine days later, blessing his son. Mercédès and M. Morrel tried to help; Morrel left a red silk purse that paid the old man’s debts and funeral. Then Caderousse names the culprits: Danglars, driven by ambition, wrote the denunciation with his left hand at La Réserve, and Fernand, driven by love, posted it. Caderousse admits he was there, drunk, and afterwards kept silent out of fear.

Morrel, who pleaded for Dantès again and again, is now nearly ruined, with every hope riding on the Pharaon. Danglars made a fortune supplying the army in Spain, married well, and is now Baron Danglars, a Paris millionaire. Fernand deserted to the enemy with a general in 1815, rose in the army, won the title Count de Morcerf in the Spanish war, served Ali Pasha in Greece, and is now a lieutenant-general with a grand house in Paris.

Mercédès, alone after Edmond vanished and his father died, eventually married Fernand in the very church where she was to have married Edmond. She educated herself, has a son, Albert, and is now a great lady, yet Caderousse believes she is unhappy; she once secretly dropped him a purse. Villefort married Mademoiselle de Saint-Méran and left Marseilles. The abbé gives Caderousse the diamond in exchange for Morrel’s red purse and rides away. La Carconte suspects the stone is fake, so Caderousse rushes off to have it valued at the Beaucaire fair.

title: The Prison Register
summary: A man posing as an English clerk of the Roman bank Thomson & French buys M. de Boville’s endangered loan to Morrel and, in return, examines the prison records, secretly pocketing Danglars’s denunciation and learning Villefort’s part in Dantès’s imprisonment.
details: The day after the visit to Caderousse, a man of about thirty-two with an English manner and accent calls on the mayor of Marseilles. He says he is chief clerk of Thomson & French, a banking house in Rome, and is worried about money lent to Morrel & Son. The mayor, himself a creditor, praises Morrel’s honesty and sends him to M. de Boville, the inspector of prisons, who has two hundred thousand francs, his daughter’s dowry, invested with Morrel. Boville is in despair: Morrel has just told him he cannot pay unless the Pharaon arrives by the 15th.

The Englishman offers to buy the debt at its full value, in cash. The only “commission” he asks is a look at the prison registers: he says he was taught in Rome by an abbé named Faria and wants to know how he died. Boville happily tells the story, including how a dangerous Bonapartist named Edmond Dantès dug a tunnel to Faria’s cell, took the dead man’s place in his burial sack, and was thrown into the sea with a cannonball tied to his feet. Boville roars with laughter, and the Englishman laughs too. Officially, Dantès is dead.

Left alone with the files, the Englishman reads Dantès’s dossier: the accusation, the record of his examination (which never mentions Noirtier), and Morrel’s petition of April 1815, exaggerated on Villefort’s advice while Napoleon ruled and later turned into a weapon against Dantès. A note in Villefort’s handwriting orders strict solitary confinement for an “inveterate Bonapartist.” Unseen, the Englishman slips Danglars’s original denunciation into his pocket, then pays Boville and receives the transfer of the debt.

title: The House of Morrel & Son
summary: The Thomson & French clerk visits the desperate Morrel, who owes 287,500 francs. News comes that the Pharaon has sunk; the stranger grants three months’ delay and tells Julie Morrel to obey a future letter signed “Sinbad the Sailor.”
details: Morrel’s once-bustling firm is almost deserted. Only two employees remain: Emmanuel, a young clerk in love with Morrel’s daughter, and the one-eyed cashier Cocles, whose faith that the firm will always pay is as fixed as his arithmetic. Morrel, now fifty and white-haired, has secretly sold his wife’s and daughter’s jewels to meet last month’s bills. Everything depends on the Pharaon, long overdue from Calcutta.

The Englishman is shown up, passing Morrel’s daughter Julie on the stairs. He reveals that his firm has bought up Morrel’s bills, Boville’s included, worth 287,500 francs, and asks frankly whether Morrel can pay. Morrel admits that if the Pharaon is lost he will have to stop payment. At that moment Julie bursts in weeping: the Pharaon has sunk, though the crew was rescued by another ship. The old sailor Penelon tells of the storm, of Captain Gaumard’s courage, and of three days adrift without food; the Englishman, clearly an expert seaman, comments on the handling of the ship.

Morrel pays the sailors what he can, and they generously offer to wait for the rest. Alone with Morrel, the Englishman, moved to tears, grants three months’ grace, renewing the bills until 5 September at eleven o’clock. Morrel thanks him, privately vowing to pay or die. On the stairs the stranger tells Julie that one day she will receive a letter signed “Sinbad the Sailor,” which she must obey exactly, however strange, and hints that she will marry Emmanuel. Then he asks Penelon for a word in private.

title: The Fifth of September
summary: Facing bankruptcy, Morrel prepares to shoot himself at eleven. At the last moment Julie brings a red purse holding his paid bill and a diamond for her dowry, and a new Pharaon sails in. The unknown benefactor departs, turning now to vengeance.
details: The delay lets Morrel scrape through June, July, and August, paying bills against everyone’s expectations. Captain Gaumard returns, and Morrel notices Penelon, newly dressed and oddly embarrassed, and assumes he has found a new master. Morrel’s last hope, a trip to Paris to ask Danglars, who owes his start in life to Morrel, ends in a humiliating refusal. Julie writes to her brother Maximilian, a principled young army officer nicknamed “the stoic,” to come home, and Madame Morrel sees her husband writing what looks like his will.

On the morning of 5 September, Maximilian arrives and discovers pistols under his father’s coat. Morrel shows him the books: 287,500 francs owed, about 15,000 in hand. Dying, Morrel says, he leaves an honest name; living, he would only be a bankrupt. Maximilian accepts, takes off his epaulets, and promises to live for his mother and sister and to repay every debt, starting with Thomson & French. Morrel waits alone as the clock nears eleven, the pistol in his mouth.

Meanwhile a messenger with an Italian accent hands Julie a letter from “Sinbad the Sailor” telling her to fetch a red silk purse from a fifth-floor room at 15 Allées de Meilhan, Dantès’s father’s old home. She bursts in just in time: the purse, Morrel’s own long-lost one, holds the receipted bill and a huge diamond labelled “Julie’s Dowry.” Then Emmanuel shouts that the Pharaon is entering the harbor: an exact copy of the lost ship, cargo and all, with Gaumard and Penelon aboard. Hidden in the crowd, a man with a black beard blesses Morrel, calls for Jacopo, and boards his yacht, declaring that, having rewarded the good, he will now punish the wicked.

title: Italy: Sinbad the Sailor
summary: In 1838 Franz d’Épinay, on his way to meet Albert de Morcerf for the Roman Carnival, lands on Monte Cristo, where a mysterious host calling himself “Sinbad the Sailor” entertains him in a hidden underground palace and offers him hashish.
details: Years have passed. Early in 1838 two young Parisian aristocrats, Viscount Albert de Morcerf and Baron Franz d’Épinay, plan to see the Carnival in Rome and book rooms with Signor Pastrini at the Hôtel de Londres. While Albert visits Naples, Franz tours Elba and, after poor hunting on Pianosa, accepts his boat captain Gaetano’s suggestion to hunt wild goats on the uninhabited island of Monte Cristo, in spite of grim stories about pirates who sink ships with their crews aboard.

At night they see a fire on the shore. Gaetano swims in to scout and reports Spanish smugglers with two Corsican bandits, men he treats as fellow sailors. Franz is made welcome, and the smugglers’ chief invites him to supper, on condition that he is blindfolded. The sailors say the chief calls himself Sinbad the Sailor, owns a fast Genoese yacht, and lives in a cave more splendid than any palace.

With the blindfold removed, Franz meets a strikingly handsome man of about forty in Tunisian dress, deathly pale, in rooms full of crimson brocade, marble statues, and treasures. Franz takes the name Aladdin for the evening. Ali, a mute Nubian whom Sinbad saved from the Bey of Tunis, serves a lavish supper. Sinbad speaks of vows still to be fulfilled, of dispensing his own secret justice, and of going to Paris one day; when Franz guesses at revenge, his host laughs it off. Then Sinbad offers him hashish, and Franz sinks into a wild, sensual dream in which the statues come to life.

title: The Waking
summary: Franz wakes in a bare grotto to find that Sinbad has sailed away. Unable to find the secret entrance, he leaves the island and travels to Rome, where he joins Albert at Signor Pastrini’s crowded hotel on the eve of Carnival.
details: Franz wakes on a bed of heather in an ordinary-looking grotto, his head clear and the dream of the statues gone. Gaetano passes on Sinbad’s apologies: urgent business has called him to Malaga. Through his telescope Franz sees his host standing on the deck of his yacht, waving farewell, and hears a small gun fired in salute.

Franz spends hours searching the cave walls with a torch and his hunting knife, but finds no trace of the hidden door, only smoke marks left by others who have tried. He notices the yacht heading for Corsica, not Malaga, and Gaetano explains that Sinbad is landing the two Corsican bandits: he is said to fear neither God nor devil and will sail far out of his way to help a hunted man. With nothing more to learn, Franz sails off, and the whole adventure begins to feel like a dream.

After finishing his business in Florence, Franz reaches Rome just before the Carnival, with the streets packed. Signor Pastrini welcomes him and Albert to their small rooms; the rest of the floor has been taken by a very rich gentleman thought to be Sicilian or Maltese. Pastrini warns that carriages and horses are impossible to find, but Albert, sure that a full purse solves everything, goes happily to bed.

title: Roman Bandits
summary: Signor Pastrini warns Franz and Albert about the bandit Luigi Vampa and tells his story: a gifted shepherd who loved Teresa, killed the bandit chief Cucumetto, and took over his band. Franz is startled to hear that Vampa once met a traveller called Sinbad the Sailor.
details: Pastrini can find the friends a carriage only until Sunday, and windows overlooking the Corso are all taken. When Franz plans a moonlight drive outside the city walls to the Colosseum, Pastrini warns them about Luigi Vampa, a young bandit who kills prisoners whose ransom arrives late. Albert scoffs, but Franz wants to hear more; Pastrini knew Vampa as a child and was once captured and freed by him, receiving a fine watch as a gift.

Vampa was a shepherd boy on the Count of San-Felice’s farm, astonishingly quick: he taught himself to read and write, carved wood beautifully, and became a deadly shot. He grew up beside Teresa, a beautiful, vain orphan shepherdess, and they planned to marry. Pastrini also describes the brutal bandit chief Cucumetto, including the story of Carlini, a bandit who stabbed his beloved Rita to save her from the band. Vampa and Teresa once hid Cucumetto from soldiers and refused his gold, though Teresa’s eyes lit up at the sight of it.

At the count’s Carnival ball, Teresa dances with nobles alongside the count’s daughter Carmela, and Vampa burns with jealousy. That night the villa catches fire; an unknown peasant rescues Carmela, and next day Vampa presents Teresa with Carmela’s costume and jewels. While guiding a lost traveller, who gives his name as Sinbad the Sailor, Vampa hears Teresa scream: Cucumetto is carrying her off. Vampa shoots him dead, puts on his clothes, and leads Teresa to the bandits, who make him their captain. Franz, struck by the name Sinbad, decides they will drive to the Colosseum through the city streets.

title: The Colosseum
summary: At the Colosseum Franz overhears a cloaked man with Sinbad’s voice promise a bandit to save the condemned Peppino. At the opera he sees the same man with a beautiful Greek girl; next morning the friends call on their neighbour, the Count of Monte Cristo.
details: In the moonlit Colosseum, Franz slips away from the guides and, hidden behind a pillar, watches a cloaked man meet a peasant from the Trastevere district, who drops in through a hole in the roof. Two men are to be executed in two days, the peasant reports: a murderer and Peppino, a shepherd whose only crime was supplying food to the peasant’s band. He plans to rescue Peppino by force; the cloaked man promises instead to buy a pardon, and will signal success by hanging the middle one of three windows he has rented on the Corso with white damask and a red cross. In return the peasant swears absolute obedience. Franz recognizes the voice as Sinbad’s.

Next evening at the Teatro Argentina, Albert, stung at having had no romantic adventures in Italy, gets Franz to introduce him to the Venetian Countess G——. In a box opposite, Franz sees a lovely woman in Greek dress with a motionless man in the shadows behind her. When the man stands, Franz recognizes Sinbad. The countess, shuddering at his pallor, calls him a vampire, “Lord Ruthven himself,” and makes Franz escort her home. Albert later reports that the man spoke modern Greek and was very elegantly dressed.

Back at the hotel, Pastrini announces that the Count of Monte Cristo, who has the rest of their floor, offers them seats in his carriage and at his windows in the Rospoli Palace, and the count’s servant brings his cards. Next morning the posted execution notice names Andrea Rondolo and Peppino, and Franz concludes that the peasant was Luigi Vampa himself. When the friends call on the count, Franz recognizes him as the man from the Colosseum, the theatre, and Monte Cristo.

title: La Mazzolata
summary: The Count of Monte Cristo entertains Franz and Albert, sets out a chilling philosophy of revenge, and takes them to watch the executions. Peppino is pardoned at the scaffold; the murderer Andrea, raging, is clubbed and stabbed to death while the count looks on in triumph.
details: The count greets the friends warmly, gives no sign of knowing Franz, and summons his steward Bertuccio, who looks exactly like the smuggler who led Franz into the cave on Monte Cristo, to confirm his window over the Piazza del Popolo. Reading Franz’s copy of the execution notice, the count remarks that he has heard Peppino may be pardoned.

When the talk turns to punishment, the count says he has seen the tortures of nearly every nation. With sudden hatred in his face, he argues that the guillotine is too quick a pain for someone who has caused years of suffering, such as destroying a man’s father, mother, or betrothed, and that a duel is no true revenge either; slow, deep torment should be repaid in kind, “an eye for an eye.” Albert simply enjoys the breakfast and the count’s cigars, but Franz notices that the count barely eats and keeps looking intently at Albert. The count says he will visit Paris soon, and Albert promises to return his hospitality there.

On the way, Franz sees the count’s three windows on the Corso: two hung with yellow damask and the middle one white with a red cross. The count has kept his promise. From their window they watch the procession of penitents, the executioner with his heavy mallet, and the two prisoners. As Peppino reaches the scaffold, a pardon is read out. Andrea, the murderer, goes berserk, screaming that Peppino must die with him, and the count laughs bitterly at this proof of human nature. Andrea is struck down with the mallet and his throat is cut. Franz half faints and Albert clings to the curtains, while the count stands upright “like the Avenging Angel.”

title: The Carnival at Rome
summary: The Carnival begins. Albert flirts with a masked peasant woman who throws him violets and sends him a note arranging a meeting. The count lends the friends his carriage and box but remains an enigma to Franz. On the last night Albert vanishes with his mysterious beauty.
details: As Franz recovers, the count is already changing into costume; Peppino, he says, slipped away in the crowd. The friends throw themselves into the Corso’s mad battle of confetti and flowers in the count’s carriage. The count leaves them at the Rospoli Palace, where Franz imagines that the figure in a blue domino (a hooded masquerade cloak) at the window is the Greek girl. Albert catches the eye of a woman in a carriage full of Roman peasants, who throws him a bunch of violets.

At the theatre Franz tells the Countess G—— that the count is a Tuscan count named after the island he bought, and she decides her vampire is just an eccentric millionaire. Over the next days the count lends the friends his carriage freely and impresses them with his knowledge of literature, painting, and chemistry. Albert’s flirtation grows: the woman lifts her mask and is charming, and Albert, sure she is a noblewoman, writes to her. Her elegant reply tells him to follow the peasant who snatches his candle at the church of San Giacomo on Tuesday evening. Franz, meanwhile, is received by Pope Gregory XVI.

To Franz the count is a puzzle out of Byron: he must know Franz recognizes him, yet he never mentions their earlier meetings. Franz admires him but does not want to be in Paris when he arrives there. On Tuesday, the last day, after the horse races, the Corso blazes with thousands of moccoletti, small candles that everyone tries to blow out. At seven, Albert, dressed as a harlequin with rose ribbons, has his candle snatched by a masked peasant woman and disappears with her toward the Via Macello. Then the bell sounds, every light goes out, and the Carnival is over.

title: The Catacombs of Saint Sebastian
summary: A ransom note reveals that Luigi Vampa has kidnapped Albert. Franz turns to the count, who, guided by Peppino, takes him to the bandits’ lair in the catacombs, where Vampa apologizes and frees Albert at once. Franz notices the count shudder as he shakes Albert’s hand.
details: Albert does not come back. At the Duke of Bracciano’s ball Franz learns that a man has brought a letter from Albert. It asks for four thousand piastres; beneath it, a note signed Luigi Vampa says that if the money is not paid by six in the morning, Albert will die at seven. Franz is several hundred piastres short and goes to the count, who offers his gold freely. Franz suggests a better way: the count saved Peppino’s life, so surely Vampa will release Albert for him.

The count calls up the cloaked messenger, who turns out to be Peppino and falls to his knees in gratitude. He explains the trap: Vampa himself drove the peasants’ carriage, Teresa flirted with Albert with his consent, and the “peasant girl” at San Giacomo was Beppo, a fifteen-year-old boy, who led Albert into an ambush outside the walls. Ali, the mute servant from Monte Cristo, drives the count, Franz, and Peppino out along the Appian Way to the catacombs of Saint Sebastian.

Through dark tunnels they reach a burial chamber where Vampa sits reading among twenty bandits. When the guns are raised, the count calmly reproaches Vampa for breaking their agreement that the count’s friends would be respected. Vampa, mortified, threatens his own men and apologizes. Albert is found sound asleep, dreaming of a dance with the Countess G——, and accepts his release with perfect coolness, thanking the count and lighting his cigar from Vampa’s torch. Vampa tells Franz his favorite book is Caesar’s Commentaries. By two o’clock Albert is dancing at the ball, while Franz wonders why the count shuddered when he had to take Albert’s hand.

title: The Rendezvous
summary: In Rome, the Count of Monte Cristo asks Albert to introduce him to Paris society, and they fix a precise appointment: 21 May, 10:30 a.m., at Albert's home. Franz, uneasy, tells Albert everything he knows about the Count, but Albert brushes his fears aside.
details: The morning after his rescue from the bandits, Albert de Morcerf, with Franz d'Épinay, goes to thank the Count of Monte Cristo again and offers the help of his family, including his father, the Comte de Morcerf, a man of Spanish origin with influence in Paris and Madrid. The Count accepts at once: he has never seen Paris, he says, and needs someone to open the doors of fashionable society to him. Albert mentions that his father has called him home to arrange a marriage.

The Count, insisting on his punctuality, sets the meeting three months ahead: the 21st of May at half-past ten in the morning, at Albert's rooms, No. 27 Rue du Helder. Franz watches him closely, remembering the plans the Count hinted at in the grotto of Monte Cristo. When they shake hands on parting, the Count's hand feels as cold as a corpse's.

Alone with Albert, Franz breaks his silence and tells him everything: the island, the smugglers and Corsican bandits, the enchanted underground palace, the hashish, the conversation he overheard at the Colosseum between the Count and Vampa, and how the Count freed Albert. Albert explains it all away. Rich men own yachts and take titles from land they buy, Corsican bandits are just outlaws, and in any case the Count saved his life and 4,000 piastres without asking a single question. Franz gives up the argument, though he still calls the Count a most singular man.
The next day the friends part, Albert for Paris and Franz for Venice. Before leaving, Albert leaves a card for the Count with the address and date written on it.

title: The Guests
summary: In Paris on the morning of 21 May, Albert prepares a breakfast for the Count in his elegant bachelor pavilion. His first guests arrive: Lucien Debray, a minister's private secretary, and Beauchamp, a newspaper editor.
details: The scene moves to Paris. Albert lives in a pavilion in the courtyard of his parents' grand house, the home of the Count and Countess of Morcerf, a place clearly chosen by a loving mother who wanted to keep her son close while giving him his freedom. The narrator describes his rooms in detail: a private side door, a smoking room stocked with every kind of tobacco, and a studio crammed with musical instruments, paintings, fencing gear, armor, antiques and stuffed birds, the remains of a string of passing hobbies.

At a quarter to ten his valet Germain brings the post. Albert accepts a seat in Madame Danglars' opera box and asks for a liqueur set from his mother, telling her he will introduce someone to her that afternoon. He admits he does not fully trust the Count to keep the appointment, but means to be punctual himself.

Lucien Debray arrives first, a cool, fashionable young man who is private secretary to the Minister of the Interior. He has been up all night writing dispatches about Spanish affairs, and mentions that the banker M. Danglars somehow learned the news early and made a million on the stock exchange. He also says he dined the night before at M. de Villefort's. Beauchamp, a journalist on an opposition paper, comes next, and the two trade friendly political insults while Albert waits for his last two guests.

title: The Breakfast
summary: Château-Renaud arrives with Captain Maximilian Morrel, who saved his life in Algeria. As the clock strikes half-past ten the Count of Monte Cristo appears, dazzles the company, reacts with visible emotion to Morrel, and reveals he already has a house in Paris.
details: While they wait, the guests gossip about Albert's expected engagement to Eugénie Danglars, daughter of the newly made Baron Danglars. Château-Renaud, a nobleman of old family, arrives with Maximilian Morrel, a captain of Spahis (French cavalry in Algeria). Morrel saved Château-Renaud from Arab horsemen on the 5th of September, a date he honors each year as the anniversary of the day his father was miraculously saved. Albert then tells his own story of being kidnapped in Rome and set free by the Count of Monte Cristo. The others laugh at it, though Morrel remarks that Monte Cristo is a small island he has heard old sailors such as Penelon talk about.

On the stroke of half-past ten the Count enters without a sound. He greets everyone politely and coolly, but at Morrel's name he steps forward and colors, and his voice trembles as he praises Morrel's noble heart. At table he eats little, shows off an emerald box of opium-and-hashish pills, mentions gifts of emeralds to the Sultan and the Pope, explains how he once captured Vampa and let him go, and declares he protects no society that does not protect him.

The Count says he has a credit with Baron Danglars through several banks, among them Thomson & French of Rome. Morrel starts at that name: this firm once did his family a great service and has always denied it. Each guest suggests a district for the Count to live in, and Morrel offers rooms at his sister Julie's house, where she lives happily with her husband Emmanuel Herbaut. The Count declines. His mute Nubian servant Ali has already bought and furnished a house on the Champs-Élysées, his steward Bertuccio has taken boxes at the theatres, and he mentions a Greek slave. Morrel leaves his card, and the Count promises to visit.

title: The Presentation
summary: Albert shows the Count his rooms and introduces him to his parents. The Count goes pale before a portrait of Albert's mother in Catalan dress; the Countess is Mercédès. Afterwards she questions Albert anxiously about the Count and warns him to be careful.
details: Albert takes the Count around his rooms and finds that his guest knows the date and origin of every object and the painter of every picture. In the bedroom the Count stops dead before a portrait of a dark-eyed young woman in the dress of a Catalan fisherwoman, gazing at the sea. He turns pale and breathes hard, then calmly calls her a charming mistress. Albert explains that it is his mother. His father dislikes the portrait, and his mother rarely looks at it without crying.

In the main house the Count admires the Morcerf coat of arms with hidden irony and meets the Count of Morcerf, a general and peer of France who looks older than his years and whose worn face seems to the Count to tell a story of secret troubles. Morcerf explains that he left the army after the July Revolution of 1830 and went into politics. The Count flatters him lavishly. Then the Countess appears in the doorway, pale and motionless. The narrator names her: Mercédès. She thanks the Count for saving her son, and he, even paler than she is, bows deeply. He declines her invitation to stay and leaves in a splendid new carriage, noticing as he goes that the curtain of her window moves.

Albert finds his mother lying in a darkened room, smelling salts beside her, blaming the strong scent of the flowers. She asks whether Monte Cristo is a real name, how old the Count is (thirty-five, Albert thinks, which seems to shock her), and whether he is really what he appears to be. She urges Albert to be prudent, then asks how his father received the guest. Albert thinks she has fallen asleep and tiptoes out, concluding that if his mother noticed the Count, he must be remarkable.

title: Monsieur Bertuccio
summary: At his new house on the Champs-Élysées, the Count buys a country house at Auteuil without looking at it. His steward Bertuccio turns pale at the address, and the Count insists that Bertuccio come with him to see it that same evening.
details: The Count arrives at the house Ali has chosen for him on the Champs-Élysées, where Ali and his steward Bertuccio are waiting. Bertuccio reports that the Count's new visiting cards have been engraved and the first one taken to Baron Danglars. A notary is waiting to complete the sale of a country house the Count wants to buy.

The Count claims not to know where the house is. When the notary says Auteuil, just outside Paris, Bertuccio goes pale and suggests several better places instead. The Count signs anyway, pays more than the asking price, and sends the delighted notary away.

Alone, the Count unlocks a private notebook he keeps on a key round his neck and checks the address in the deed against his notes: 'Auteuil, Rue de la Fontaine, No. 28; it is indeed the same.' He wonders aloud whether he can trust a confession 'extorted by religious or physical terror', and says that within an hour he will know everything. He then asks Bertuccio whether he knows the area around Paris. Bertuccio, trembling, says no, and is horrified to learn that he must come to Auteuil at once. The steward, who has never dared to disobey, follows his master into the carriage.

title: The House at Auteuil
summary: At the Auteuil house, which once belonged to the Marquis de Saint-Méran, the terrified Bertuccio admits that he committed a killing in its garden as an act of revenge, and that his victim was M. de Villefort.
details: Bertuccio crosses himself in the Corsican way and grows more frightened as they drive into Auteuil. The caretaker tells them the house's former owner was the Marquis de Saint-Méran, a loyal Bourbon supporter whose only daughter married M. de Villefort, once the king's attorney at Nîmes, and died twenty-one years ago. Bertuccio has to lean on the wall to stay upright.

The Count makes Bertuccio light the way through the house and down a private staircase into the garden. There Bertuccio freezes and begs his master to move away from a certain spot, the place where 'he fell'. The Count coldly threatens to send him to an asylum or dismiss him. He reminds Bertuccio that he came to him with a letter of recommendation from the Abbé Busoni, who heard his confession in prison at Nîmes, and he says he will hold the abbé responsible.

Desperate not to lose his position, Bertuccio admits that he committed a vendetta (a Corsican blood revenge) in this very garden, and that two steps from the spot is the grave in which the victim had just buried his child. He says the Count, standing in his cloak under the plane tree, reminds him of the man: M. de Villefort, the magistrate with the spotless reputation, who was, Bertuccio says, a villain. The Count sits down on a bench, humming an opera tune, and orders him to tell the whole story.

title: The Vendetta
summary: Bertuccio tells his story: Villefort refused justice for his murdered brother, so he declared a vendetta, stabbed Villefort in the Auteuil garden, and saved the baby Villefort was burying. Years later, hiding at Caderousse's inn, he watched Caderousse sell the abbé's diamond to a jeweller.
details: In 1815 Bertuccio's elder brother, a Corsican officer of Napoleon's army, was murdered in Nîmes during the royalist massacres. Bertuccio begged the king's attorney there, Villefort, to find the killers and to grant the widow, Assunta, a pension. Villefort dismissed the dead man as a soldier of 'the usurper' and threatened to throw Bertuccio out, so Bertuccio declared a vendetta against him. He followed Villefort to Versailles and discovered his secret visits to the Auteuil house, where a young, pregnant woman known only as 'the Baroness' was living.

One stormy September night Bertuccio hid in the garden and saw Villefort come out with a spade and bury a box. He stabbed him and dug up the box, thinking it held treasure. Inside was a newborn baby, nearly suffocated. Bertuccio revived it and left it at the foundling hospital in Paris, keeping half of its linen, which was marked with an H and an N under a baron's coronet. Assunta later reclaimed the boy and named him Benedetto. He grew up charming but wicked, stealing and lying, and once taunted Bertuccio that he was not his father.

In June 1829, while running from customs officers, Bertuccio hid in a shed beside Gaspard Caderousse's inn on the Beaucaire road. Through the wall he watched Caderousse and his wife, La Carconte, sell a diamond to a Paris jeweller named Joannes. It had been left to them, they said, by a sailor named Edmond Dantès and delivered by an Abbé Busoni. The jeweller paid 45,000 francs and set off into a storm, ignoring the couple's greedy whispers. Then a knock came: Joannes was back, asking to spend the night.

title: The Rain of Blood
summary: Bertuccio finishes his tale: the Caderousses murdered the jeweller, Caderousse fled, and Bertuccio was arrested for the crime until the Abbé Busoni came to his aid. Benedetto later tortured Assunta for money and vanished. That night Haydée arrives at the Count's Paris house.
details: La Carconte fawned over the jeweller and put him to bed. Bertuccio dozed off and woke to a pistol shot, screams and a struggle overhead, and warm drops falling on his face through the floor. Caderousse came down covered in blood, took the diamond and the money, and fled. Bertuccio broke through to help and found La Carconte shot dead on the stairs and Joannes dying of knife wounds. Customs officers and gendarmes burst in, found Bertuccio soaked in blood, and arrested him.

In prison at Nîmes he begged the authorities to find the Abbé Busoni. After three months the abbé appeared, confirmed the diamond story, and heard Bertuccio's confession, including the Auteuil killing. Caderousse was later caught, confessed, and was sent to the galleys for life, and Bertuccio was freed. The abbé then recommended him to the Count. Back in Corsica, Bertuccio found that Benedetto and two companions had held Assunta over a fire to make her reveal where her money was hidden, then robbed the house and disappeared. She died of her burns. 'Those Villeforts are an accursed race,' Bertuccio says, and the Count murmurs agreement.

The Count tells him that his real crime was not returning the rescued baby to its mother, and that the wicked are not so easily gone: Benedetto may be alive. He sends Bertuccio away, studies the garden as a 'plan' laid out before him, and murmurs that the prosecutor may not be dead. Back on the Champs-Élysées, he moves through the house as if he has always known it, and at midnight welcomes Haydée, the beautiful young Greek woman from Italy, to her secret apartments.

title: Unlimited Credit
summary: Baron Danglars calls at the Count's house and is turned away. The Count has Danglars' prized horses bought out from under him, then visits the banker and crushes his doubts about an 'unlimited' credit, arranging to draw six million francs in the first year.
details: Baron Danglars, a showy, sly-looking man past fifty with dyed hair, drives up and is told the Count is not receiving. From behind his blinds the Count studies him through a lorgnette and remarks on his 'decidedly bad countenance'. He orders Bertuccio to buy Danglars' fine horses at double the price, and reassures the anxious Ali kindly in Arabic. He tells his valet Baptistin that he must never gossip about his master, and adds that he keeps a fund for loyal servants. Ali, he says, is not a servant but a slave whose life is his. He also orders Bertuccio to find him an estate on the Normandy coast with a harbor for his corvette, and to keep his ships and relays of horses ready.

At five o'clock the Count drives to Danglars' house in the Chaussée d'Antin behind the banker's own horses. Danglars has just told his colleagues he suspects a hoax: Thomson & French of Rome have given this so-called count unlimited credit with him. In his gaudy white-and-gold drawing room he tries to patronize the Count, who mocks his titles. When Danglars grandly offers 'even a million', the Count pulls two treasury notes of 500,000 francs each from his card case and shows further letters of unlimited credit on Rothschild and Lafitte.

Danglars is overwhelmed. They settle on six million francs for the year, beginning with 500,000 the next morning. The Count says his fortune is an old family treasure only recently released to him, and adds, with a ghastly smile, that Danglars will soon know more about him. Danglars offers to present him to the Baroness, who is with Lucien Debray. The Count smiles, since he already knows the banker's domestic secrets.

title: The Dappled Grays
summary: Madame Danglars is furious that her husband sold her dappled grays, now pulling the Count's carriage. The Count returns them decorated with diamonds. Next day the horses bolt at Auteuil with Madame de Villefort and her son aboard, and Ali stops them.
details: The Count is presented to Madame Danglars in her pink boudoir, where Debray is also present. She has heard all about the Count from Debray and Albert. Her maid then reports that her pair of dappled gray horses, promised for Madame de Villefort's drive the next day, have vanished from the stable. Danglars stammers excuses and whispers that he sold them at a huge profit, just as Debray spots the grays harnessed to the Count's carriage outside. Debray slips away before the quarrel breaks out, and the Count leaves pleased: 'The domestic peace of this family is henceforth in my hands.'
