Two hours later he sends the horses back with a large diamond fixed in each rosette of their harness.

At Auteuil the next day the Count asks Ali whether his lasso could stop two runaway horses, and stations him outside the house. At five o'clock the grays come racing by, out of control, carrying a young woman and a small boy. Ali lassoes one horse and grips the other by the nostrils. The Count carries the pair inside and revives the unconscious boy with a single drop of a blood-red elixir.

The lady is Héloïse de Villefort, wife of the king's attorney, and the boy is her spoiled son Edward, who goes straight for the Count's bottles of drugs and calls Ali 'too ugly' to thank. The Count warns that some of the liquids are dangerous even to smell, and notices her glance at the case. Ali drives them home behind the now sluggish horses. She writes to her friend Hermine Danglars, begging to meet the Count again, and all Paris talks of the adventure. That night M. de Villefort, in full dress, calls at the Count's house.

title: Ideology
summary: Villefort, now a cold, powerful royal prosecutor in Paris, comes to thank the Count. They spar about justice: the Count calls himself an agent of Providence sent to reward and punish, and Villefort answers with the story of his father Noirtier, struck down by paralysis.
details: The narrator describes M. de Villefort as he is now. He is a respected and much-feared king's attorney who has survived four revolutions, rarely pays visits, runs a stiff, correct household with his young wife and his daughter by his first marriage, and despises dreamers and theories. He has grown thin and yellow, wears gold spectacles and dresses all in black. He arrives suspecting the Count is an adventurer or an escaped criminal.

The Count meets his stiff thanks with a chilly reply and then a string of provocations. He has studied the laws of every nation and found the primitive law of retaliation closest to God's law. There are men, he says, whom God sends with a mission rather than a post, and he is one of them, a man of no country, stopped only by death. Asked his ambition, he tells a parable: Satan offered him the world, and he answered that he wished to be Providence, because nothing is finer than to reward and punish. He was made one of Providence's agents, and would make the same bargain again. He adds that he has been 'nearly mad' once.

Shaken, Villefort warns him that worse things than death exist, such as apoplexy (a stroke). He describes his father, M. Noirtier, once a fearless Jacobin and Bonapartist plotter, now paralyzed and speechless overnight and dependent on his granddaughter Valentine. Villefort calls this God's punishment of his father alone, while his children Valentine and Edward are his compensation. The Count smiles while groaning inwardly, promises to visit, and, once Villefort leaves, says: 'Enough of this poison, let me now seek the antidote.'

title: Haydée
summary: Before visiting the Morrels, the Count spends an hour with Haydée in her Eastern apartments. He tells her she is free in France and may leave him; she insists she will never leave him. He asks her to keep the secret of her birth.
details: After Villefort's visit the Count looks forward to calling on old friends in the Rue Meslay: Maximilian, Julie and Emmanuel. To prepare himself, he first spends an hour with Haydée. She lives in rooms furnished in Eastern style, with Turkish carpets and silk divans, and has three French maids and a Greek one, all ordered to treat her like a queen. The narrator describes her: about nineteen or twenty, dressed in the costume of Epirus (a region of north-western Greece), smoking a narghile (water pipe), strikingly beautiful.

She greets him in Greek, asking why he asks permission to enter when he is her master. The Count tells her that in France she is free, free even to leave him, and that she may find someone she prefers. Haydée answers that she has loved no one but him and her father, and that her love for him is not a daughter's love: if he died, she would die too.

He gives her full freedom of the house, a carriage, and Ali and her maid Myrtho to go with her. He asks only one thing: that she keep the secret of her birth and never speak the names of her 'illustrious father' or 'ill-fated mother'. He then leaves for the Morrels', murmuring lines of Pindar about youth and love.

title: The Morrel Family
summary: The Count visits Maximilian, Julie and Emmanuel, whose happiness moves him deeply. They show him relics of their unknown benefactor, 'Sinbad the Sailor'. He suggests a 'Lord Wilmore', then leaves abruptly on hearing old Morrel died believing their rescuer was Edmond Dantès.
details: The Morrels' house in the Rue Meslay is cheerful and comfortable. The one-eyed Cocles, now the doorkeeper, does not recognize the Count, and the old sailor Penelon is the gardener. Maximilian explains that his father died leaving 500,000 francs. Julie and her husband Emmanuel worked until they had earned 250,000 francs more, then closed the firm rather than risk the Morrel name, and now live happily on a modest income.

The Count is so moved by their contentment that he can barely speak. Julie says that God once sent them an angel. Under a glass cover they keep their dearest treasures: a silk purse, a letter signed 'Sinbad the Sailor', and the diamond given to Julie as her dowry. These are relics of the stranger who saved their father from suicide and the firm from ruin. They have never been able to thank him. Penelon once glimpsed the Englishman who visited in 1829, a clerk from Thomson & French, boarding a yacht at Trieste.

The Count, uneasy under Julie's gaze, describes the Englishman exactly, then claims he must have been a friend of his, an eccentric Lord Wilmore who did such kindnesses secretly and did not believe in gratitude. He says Wilmore has left for distant lands and will never return. Maximilian adds that their father always said 'It was no Englishman', and that his last words were 'Maximilian, it was Edmond Dantès!' The Count goes deathly pale, makes hurried excuses and leaves. Julie says his voice seemed familiar.

title: Pyramus and Thisbe
summary: Maximilian Morrel and Valentine de Villefort, secretly in love, meet at a boarded-up gate in her family's garden. Valentine, unhappily engaged to Franz d'Épinay, describes her lonely home life and odd reactions to Morrel's name. The Count's arrival interrupts them.
details: Behind a grand house in the Faubourg Saint-Honoré, a disused gate separates the garden from an abandoned vegetable plot. Here a young woman waits by the planks, and a tall young man in a workman's blouse slips in to meet her: Maximilian Morrel and Valentine de Villefort. (The chapter takes its title from Pyramus and Thisbe, lovers in an old legend who talked through a crack in a wall.) To meet her safely, Maximilian has rented the plot as a 'gardener' for 500 francs a year.

Valentine is afraid. She is engaged to Franz d'Épinay, and her father never changes his mind. At home she feels like an outcast: her father ignores her, and her stepmother hates her behind constant smiles, perhaps because Valentine has her own mother's fortune and will inherit from her grandparents, the Saint-Mérans, while Madame de Villefort's adored son Edward has nothing. Her only comfort is her paralyzed grandfather Noirtier, who can speak only with his eyes. Maximilian promises patience: Franz is not due back for a year.

Valentine asks whether their fathers ever quarrelled in Marseilles. When she read aloud the news of Maximilian's promotion in the Legion of Honor, her father started and sneered at the Bonapartist Morrels of 1815, and she thought M. Danglars, who was present, trembled too. Noirtier, however, signalled with his eyes that he was glad of Maximilian's honor. A maid then calls Valentine indoors: the Count of Monte Cristo has come to call. Maximilian wonders how the Count knows M. de Villefort.

title: Toxicology
summary: The Count calls on Madame de Villefort and reminds her that they once discussed poisons at Perugia. She eagerly draws him out on how poisons can kill without leaving traces, and he gives her a dangerous elixir, pleased that 'the seed sown' has found fertile soil.
details: Villefort is out, so Madame de Villefort receives the Count with Edward, who torments a parrot and tears up an album while his mother barely scolds him. Valentine comes in, sad and recently in tears. The Count claims to remember them all from Perugia two years earlier, and Madame de Villefort finally recalls talking at length with a man in a long cloak she took for a doctor. They had discussed the famous aqua Tofana, a legendary Italian poison, and she had asked about Valentine's health. At six o'clock she sends Valentine off to give Noirtier his dinner and sends Edward after her, closing the door carefully.

Alone with the Count, she returns again and again to poison. The Count explains how Mithridates, an ancient king, made himself immune by taking small, increasing doses; how Eastern poisoners cover their tracks; and how a 'terrible chemist' he knew, the Abbé Adelmonte, poisoned a cabbage with strychnine so that, passed along a chain of animals, it left no trace except what looked like apoplexy (a stroke). She shows that she already knows a good deal of chemistry. When she raises conscience, he answers with cases of people who excused their crimes as acts of love, among them Lady Macbeth, who he says wanted a throne for her son.

She asks about the elixir that revived Edward. One drop restores life, he says, while five or six would kill and could not be tasted in a glass of wine. He offers her the recipe and leaves for the opera. She thinks he must be the Adelmonte he talks about. The Count, satisfied, reflects that 'this is a fruitful soil', and sends the prescription the next morning.

title: Robert le Diable
summary: At the opera, all Paris stares at the Count and Haydée. In Madame Danglars' box the Count meets Eugénie and the Count of Morcerf, who served Ali Pasha at Yanina. Seeing Morcerf, Haydée nearly faints: this man, she says, sold her father to the Turks.
details: At a performance of Meyerbeer's opera Robert le Diable, Albert and Château-Renaud chat loudly in the stalls. A mystery horse entered as 'Vampa' has won the Jockey Club cup, and the Countess G——, the lovely Venetian from Rome, has received the cup 'from Lord Ruthven', the vampire nickname she once gave the Count. Albert visits her and confirms that it was the Count. Madame Danglars arrives escorted by Debray (openly hinted to be her lover) with her daughter Eugénie: handsome, cold and strong-willed, gifted in music and languages, who studies with a poor young singer, Louise d'Armilly. Albert finds her beauty too severe for his taste.

The Count enters a box with Haydée, whose beauty and diamonds hold everyone's attention. In Madame Danglars' box the ladies quiz Albert about the Count. Albert then meets the Count in the corridor, who asks whether the Count of Morcerf ever comes to the opera. Later the Count visits the baroness's box, where Morcerf has now arrived. Eugénie coolly asks whether Haydée is his daughter. Madame Danglars mentions that Morcerf served Ali Tepelini, and Morcerf confirms he was inspector-general of the Pasha's troops at Yanina and owes his fortune to him.

The Count leans over the front of the box with his arm around Morcerf, just as Haydée looks across. She sees Morcerf's face next to her guardian's, cries out and falls back in her seat. The Count excuses her nerves and returns to her. Trembling, she calls Morcerf a wretch: 'he sold my father to the Turks, and the fortune he boasts of was the price of his treachery!' The Count says he heard something of this in Epirus and asks her to tell him the details some day. They leave as the fourth act begins.

title: A Flurry in Stocks
summary: Albert confides that he dreads marrying Eugénie Danglars, a match his mother opposes. Debray squirms at a joke about tricking Madame Danglars on the stock market. The Count plans an Auteuil dinner without the Morcerfs and expects Major Cavalcanti and his son Andrea.
details: Albert and Debray call on the Count. Albert explains that his father and Danglars made their fortunes in Spain, his father in the army and Danglars supplying it. He does not love Eugénie, and his mother, for reasons he cannot explain, strongly dislikes the match with the Danglars family. Albert faked an illness to delay a meeting, but the two-month postponement ends next week.

Debray works out how much Danglars made on Haitian bonds, and lets slip that it is really Madame Danglars who gambles on the stock exchange. Albert jokes that Debray, who receives government news before anyone else, should teach her a lesson by feeding her a false report so she loses money. Debray is visibly embarrassed. The Count notices it, says something quietly to Debray as he leaves, and Debray replies, 'Willingly, count; I accept.'

The Count plans a dinner at Auteuil on Saturday for the Danglars and Villefort families. He tactfully leaves out the Morcerfs so that the Countess will not see it as a marriage meeting, and Albert decides to take his mother to the seaside at Tréport. The Count declines Albert's invitation to dine with his mother: he is expecting Major Bartolomeo Cavalcanti, an Italian nobleman, and his son Andrea, a young man making his entry into Paris society with his father's millions, whom the Count has promised to look after. Albert jokingly suggests finding Andrea a rich wife such as Eugénie. He also mentions that Franz is to marry Valentine de Villefort, and that Franz's father, General d'Épinay, was assassinated in 1815 by Bonapartists. Finally the Count orders Bertuccio to redecorate the Auteuil house, but to leave the red damask bedroom and the garden exactly as they are.

title: Major Cavalcanti
summary: An elderly Italian calling himself Major Bartolomeo Cavalcanti visits Monte Cristo, sent by the Abbé Busoni. The count coaches him through a ready-made story about a long-lost son, hands him the papers and money he needs, and tells him the son is waiting next door.
details: At seven in the evening a man of about fifty-two, in an old-fashioned green coat and a cravat that looks like a noose, arrives at the count's house on the Champs-Élysées. Baptistin recognizes him from a description. He is Bartolomeo Cavalcanti, and he carries a letter from the Abbé Busoni describing him as a noble of Lucca with an income of half a million, whose one sorrow is a son stolen in childhood. A postscript gives him credit of 48,000 francs on the count.

The 'major' is comically unsure of his own story. He is not certain he was a major, is surprised to hear how rich he is, and only 'believes' his son is called Andrea. Monte Cristo smoothly supplies every detail: the boy's mother was the Marchesa Oliva Corsinari, dead these ten years, and the boy vanished at five. When the major admits he has forgotten his marriage certificate and his son's baptism record, the count produces both, saying the abbé thoughtfully sent them.

The count then advises him what to tell Parisians: the boy was simply away at school in the provinces, or, if necessary, a treacherous tutor bribed by the family's enemies carried him off. He hands over 8,000 francs on account, tells him to stop wearing his outdated costume, and informs him that his luggage, including a uniform and medals for grand occasions, is waiting at the Hôtel des Princes. Finally he announces that the son is already in the house, and goes to prepare him for the meeting.

title: Andrea Cavalcanti
summary: Monte Cristo meets 'Count Andrea Cavalcanti', who came with a letter from 'Sinbad the Sailor'. Left alone, Andrea and the major quickly admit they are both paid impostors, agree to play father and son, and are invited to dine at Auteuil.
details: In the next room waits a tall, fair young man with a red beard. His letter of introduction is signed 'Sinbad the Sailor', who, the count explains, is really an eccentric rich Englishman called Lord Wilmore; Andrea admits he once met that Englishman. He recites a fluent tale of noble birth and kidnapping, but starts in terror when told his father is in Paris. The count hints that Wilmore found him in an 'unpleasant position' and that his youth was 'stormy', advises him not to tell his romantic story, and promises him 50,000 livres a year, paid through Danglars' bank, for as long as he stays in Paris.

Through a hidden peephole the count watches the reunion. The two men embrace like actors on a stage. Then Andrea examines the papers with an expert eye and asks, in Tuscan, whether forgers are no longer sent to the galleys (prison ships and labor camps) in Italy. He asks the major how much he is paid to be his father: 50,000 francs down, while Andrea gets 50,000 a year to be his son. They compare letters, the major's from the Abbé Busoni and Andrea's from Sinbad/Lord Wilmore, both ordering them to the count on 26 May. Neither understands the scheme, but they agree to play their parts.

The count returns, slips Andrea a packet of banknotes 'from his father', and invites both to dine on Saturday at his country house at Auteuil to meet Danglars. Watching them leave arm in arm, he calls them two scoundrels and says it is a pity they are not really related. Then, finding disgust worse than hatred, he goes to visit the Morrels.

title: In the Lucern Patch
summary: At their secret meeting place by the Villefort garden gate, Valentine and Maximilian discuss her dreaded engagement to Franz, her stepmother's interest in her fortune, and Maximilian's strange trust in Monte Cristo, whom Valentine distrusts.
details: Maximilian waits at the gate beside the lucern (alfalfa) field. Valentine is late because Madame Danglars and Eugénie are visiting, and he compares the two girls as they stroll past. Alone at last, Valentine tells him Eugénie dislikes the idea of marrying Albert de Morcerf, would prefer an independent life, and almost wishes her father would lose his fortune so she could become an artist like her friend Louise d'Armilly. Maximilian brings news that Franz d'Épinay is returning to Paris, and Valentine has been summoned by Madame de Villefort about a matter concerning her fortune.

Valentine explains her stepmother's motives. A year ago Valentine proposed entering a convent, and Madame de Villefort quietly encouraged it, because Valentine is rich: she has about 50,000 livres a year from her mother and expects more from her grandparents the Saint-Mérans and from Noirtier. If she became a nun, it would all go to her father and then to little Edward. Only her paralysed grandfather's despairing look made her give up the plan.

Maximilian asks permission to confide in the Count of Monte Cristo, whom he has known barely ten days but feels oddly bound to. He believes the count arranged for him to meet the Villeforts at the coming Auteuil dinner, and even lost at cards on purpose so Maximilian could buy the horse he longed for, Médéah. Valentine says the count is too much her stepmother's friend and has never even looked at her, so Maximilian drops the idea. Before running back to the house she lets him kiss her hand through the gate.

title: M. Noirtier de Villefort
summary: Villefort and his wife tell the paralysed Noirtier that Valentine will marry Franz d'Épinay. Furious, Noirtier lets Valentine know through his eye signals that he opposes the match, and demands a notary.
details: Noirtier can neither move nor speak; only his eyes are alive. He closes them for 'yes', blinks repeatedly for 'no', raises them when he wants something, and shuts the right eye to call Valentine or the left to call Barrois, his devoted servant of twenty-five years. Only Valentine, Barrois and Villefort understand him, and Villefort rarely bothers to visit.

Sending Valentine and Barrois away, Villefort and Madame de Villefort announce that Valentine will marry within three months, and name the groom: Franz de Quesnel, Baron d'Épinay. Noirtier's eyes blaze, and he almost chokes with rage. Madame de Villefort mentions that Franz's father was assassinated in 1815. Villefort, who knows of an old political hatred between Noirtier and the elder d'Épinay, says pointedly that whoever was guilty of that murder should be glad to offer Valentine to the victim's son as a peace-offering. Noirtier answers with a look of contempt.

When Valentine comes in, she questions him patiently and learns he is upset about the marriage and does not like Franz. She confesses she does not love Franz either, and that her convent plan was really a way to escape the match. Noirtier signals that he can still help her. Reciting the alphabet and then running her finger down a dictionary, she discovers the word he wants: 'notary' (a lawyer who draws up wills and contracts). Villefort objects that the scene will be ridiculous, but Barrois marches off to fetch one.

title: The Will
summary: With Valentine as interpreter, Noirtier proves his mind is sound and dictates a will: if Valentine marries Franz d'Épinay, his 900,000 francs will go to the poor instead of to her or anyone else in the family.
details: The notary at first refuses to act for a client who cannot speak. Valentine teaches him the yes/no signals, and through the alphabet and dictionary Noirtier spells out 'will'. The impressed notary agrees, and a second notary, already fetched by Barrois, joins him. Noirtier stops them at the exact amount of his fortune, 900,000 francs, and Barrois brings a casket holding that sum in bank scrip, proving the old man knows his affairs perfectly.

Madame de Villefort assumes the money will go to Valentine, who has nursed him for six years. Noirtier refuses, though he looks at Valentine with deep tenderness. He refuses even more fiercely to leave it to Edward, and also refuses his son. Then he fixes his eyes on Valentine's hand, and she understands: it is about her marriage. He disinherits her because of the engagement to Franz; without it, she would have been his heir.

Villefort declares that he alone decides his daughter's marriage, and she will marry Franz. Noirtier says he will leave everything to charity. The notary points out that the law protects a son's share, but Villefort says he will not contest the will, since a man in his position cannot go to court against the poor. The will is drawn up, witnessed, sealed and entrusted to the family notary, M. Deschamps. Valentine weeps, Villefort bites his lips, and Madame de Villefort cannot hide her joy.

title: The Telegraph
summary: Monte Cristo visits the Villeforts just after the will is made. He draws out the story of Noirtier's feud with Franz's father, encourages Villefort to hurry the marriage, unsettles him by revealing the Auteuil house was Saint-Méran's, and leaves to visit a telegraph.
details: Villefort, still smarting from losing 900,000 francs to an 'old man in his second childhood', vows that Valentine will marry Franz anyway. While Edward pours ink into the bird's water, Madame de Villefort suggests Valentine and Noirtier planned the whole thing together. Carried away, Villefort describes his father as a Jacobin (a radical revolutionary) who plotted against the Bourbon kings and never shrank from any means. The count recalls that General d'Épinay, a secret royalist, was assassinated after leaving a Bonapartist meeting, and Villefort looks at him almost with terror. Madame de Villefort explains the marriage was meant to end the old feud.

Madame de Villefort keeps returning to how unfair it is to Edward. The count advises settling the marriage the moment Franz returns, so it cannot be undone. Villefort gratefully agrees, while his wife changes color.

Monte Cristo reminds them of Saturday's dinner at his country house in Auteuil, Rue de la Fontaine, No. 28. Villefort is visibly shaken: it is the house he once sold for M. de Saint-Méran, and he would never live in it. The count teases that if Villefort fails to come, he will suspect the house has some gloomy legend, and Villefort hastily promises to attend. The count then says he is off to see a telegraph (in this era, a chain of towers passing signals by moving arms), choosing a lonely one on the Spanish line rather than an official station.

title: How a Gardener May Get Rid of the Dormice that Eat His Peaches
summary: Monte Cristo bribes a poor telegraph operator who loves gardening to send a false signal. The fake news that Don Carlos has returned to Spain makes Danglars dump his Spanish bonds, costing him about a million francs when the story is denied.
details: At the tower of Montlhéry, the count finds a tiny, perfectly kept garden and its owner, a telegraph operator of fifty-five, fretting over stolen strawberries and the dormice that eat his fruit. He earns a thousand francs a year, repeats signals he does not understand, and likes it that way because it means he has no responsibility. For a moment the count fears he has found a man with no ambition, which would spoil his plans.

Up in the signal room, the count shows him banknotes: 15,000 francs, then 10,000 more, enough to buy a house with two acres of garden and live on the income. In return he must transmit three signals the count has drawn on a paper. Sweating and trembling, the man does it, while the next station frantically signals in confusion. The count swears he has wronged no one, and the man faints among his dried herbs.

Minutes later, Lucien Debray, the minister's secretary, rushes to Madame Danglars: her husband must sell his Spanish bonds, because Don Carlos (a rival claimant to the Spanish throne, held in France at Bourges) has escaped to Spain. Danglars sells at any price and loses 500,000 francs, and the newspaper Le Messager prints the story. Next morning the official Le Moniteur announces it was false, blamed on a signal misread in fog. The bonds rise, and with losses and missed gains Danglars is out about a million. The count tells Morrel he has just learned how a gardener may get rid of the dormice that eat his peaches.

title: Ghosts
summary: Guests arrive for Monte Cristo's dinner at Auteuil. Bertuccio, peeking in, is horrified: Madame Danglars is the pregnant woman from the garden in his story, Villefort is the man he thought he had killed, and 'Andrea Cavalcanti' is Benedetto.
details: In a few days Bertuccio has transformed the gloomy Auteuil house: full-grown trees, a fresh lawn, a library, a conservatory, the count's dogs and birds. One room alone has been left untouched, and Bertuccio passes it in terror. The count arrives with Ali.

Morrel rides up first on Médéah, followed by the Danglars' carriage escorted by Debray and Château-Renaud. The count notices Madame Danglars slip Debray a note, and sees her cast an anxious glance over the house. She asks to buy Morrel's horse, and the count rescues him by inventing a wager. Danglars, pale after his losses, is surly and absent-mindedly strips the blossoms off an orange tree. The Cavalcanti are announced, the major in uniform covered with medals; Château-Renaud remarks that Andrea looks well dressed for the first time in his life. The count tells Danglars they are enormously rich and that the son wants a Parisian wife. Then M. and Madame de Villefort arrive, Villefort's hand trembling.

Bertuccio glances through the door and gasps. The fair lady in white with diamonds, Madame Danglars, is 'the woman of the garden' who was expecting a child, and the man she was waiting for is Villefort: 'Then I did not kill him?' The count mocks him: he must have struck badly, or dreamed it all. Then the count points out Andrea, and Bertuccio mutters, 'Benedetto? Fatality!' Benedetto is the newborn Villefort buried in this very garden and Bertuccio dug up alive, the boy his sister-in-law Assunta raised. Struggling for composure, Bertuccio announces dinner.

title: The Dinner
summary: After a lavish dinner, Monte Cristo shows his guests the old red damask bedroom and a secret staircase, then announces his workmen dug up a newborn's skeleton in a box under a garden tree. Madame Danglars faints, and Villefort secretly asks to meet her.
details: Villefort sits beside Madame Danglars, and both are uneasy. The count serves an extravagant feast, including a sterlet from the Volga and a lamprey from Lake Fusaro, both brought alive in barrels, with live spares carried in to prove it. Château-Renaud remembers that the house belonged to M. de Saint-Méran and stood empty for years, looking like a place where a crime had been committed. Villefort gulps a glass of wine and says the house was part of Valentine's dowry, which makes Morrel turn pale.

The count leads everyone to a gloomy room hung with blood-red damask, whose faded portraits seem to say 'We have seen', and opens a hidden staircase. He imagines someone creeping down it one stormy night with a burden to hide. Madame Danglars nearly faints on Villefort's arm. When the count switches to picturing an honest mother's room, with a father carrying a sleeping child down the stairs, she faints outright. Madame de Villefort hands the count her smelling bottle, filled with the red liquid he once used on Edward, and mentions she has 'made the trial' he advised.

In the garden the count declares a crime was committed here. Stamping on the ground beneath a tree, he says his workman found the ironwork of a box containing the skeleton of a newborn infant. Villefort weakly asks who said the child was buried alive. The major innocently asks what happens to child-murderers in France; Danglars says their heads are cut off, and Villefort confirms it in a voice 'scarcely human'. The count stops there and serves coffee, but Villefort whispers to Madame Danglars that he must see her tomorrow in his office.

title: The Beggar
summary: Danglars, dazzled by Major Cavalcanti, drives him home. As Andrea leaves, a ragged man calls him 'Benedetto': it is Caderousse, a runaway from the Toulon prison, who demands a monthly allowance and rides back to Paris in Andrea's carriage.
details: The party breaks up. Danglars, convinced the Cavalcanti are fabulously rich nobles, is charmed by the major's diamond ring and his refusal to be impressed by anything, and offers him a seat in his carriage. They agree to meet on business the next day. Andrea, who said little at dinner and was alarmed to find the king's prosecutor among the guests, goes to his tilbury (a light two-wheeled carriage).

A huge, bony hand falls on his shoulder. A sunburnt, bearded man in rags, with a red handkerchief on his head and teeth like a wolf's, asks for a ride back to Paris and calls him 'Master Benedetto'. Andrea sends his groom away and drives off with him. Once alone, he calls the man Caderousse. They parted at the Pont du Var, where Andrea claimed he was heading for Italy; Caderousse reminds him how he used to share his soup with him and call him his child. Andrea says he was brought up in Corsica.

Caderousse asks for 150 francs a month; Andrea gives him 200 and promises the same every month. Andrea explains he has 'found his father', Major Cavalcanti, through the Count of Monte Cristo, and warns Caderousse to keep away from the count. Caderousse refuses to get down: with no papers he would be arrested at the city barrier and sent back to Toulon as convict No. 106. Andrea's hand strays to a pistol, Caderousse quietly opens a Spanish knife, and both think better of it. Wearing the groom's coat and Andrea's hat, Caderousse passes the barrier as a servant, then vanishes with both. Andrea sighs that one cannot be completely happy in this world.

title: A Conjugal Scene
summary: Debray escorts the shaken Madame Danglars home, but Danglars sends him away and coldly confronts his wife: she owes him a share of his 700,000-franc Spanish loss, and he has long known about her lovers, including Villefort.
details: Debray rides to the Danglars house and, alone with the baroness, calls her Hermine and asks what upset her at the count's; she will not say. Her maid Cornélie reports that Eugénie is in bed while Louise d'Armilly plays the piano, and the baroness jokes that Eugénie will soon ask Debray for a job at the Opera. Then Danglars walks in and, with icy politeness, makes Debray leave.

Danglars flings his wife's little dog across the room and gets to the point: he has lost 700,000 francs on the Spanish loan. He lists the tips she gave him this year, about Haitian bonds, a railway grant, and Spanish affairs overheard at the minister's, each of which earned him a fortune, and from which she received a quarter, 500,000 livres in all. The latest tip, from her talk with Debray, was false. He demands a quarter of the loss, 175,000 francs, and suggests the money has gone to Debray. He says they ceased to be husband and wife four years ago, and that he has tolerated her 'music lessons' and her 'study of diplomacy with the minister's secretary' as long as she paid for them herself. He even suspects the minister and Debray of faking the telegraph to ruin him; she points out that the operator has fled.

Danglars boasts that for sixteen years he has seen every step she took, and that all her friends, 'from M. de Villefort to M. Debray', have trembled before him. At Villefort's name she turns white. He says her first husband, M. de Nargonne, died of grief or rage when he came home after nine months away to find her six months pregnant. Debray must pay his share or disappear. Danglars leaves her half-fainting, thinking of Villefort and the dinner.

title: Matrimonial Projects
summary: Danglars, reeling from new losses, visits Monte Cristo, who calls his wealth 'third-rate'. Danglars admits he now prefers rich Andrea Cavalcanti to Albert for Eugénie, sneers that Morcerf was once the fisherman Fernand Mondego, and on the count's hint writes to Yanina.
details: The next day Debray does not call and Madame Danglars goes out alone. Major Cavalcanti visits Danglars to cash his draft. Danglars then drives to the Chamber of Deputies and on to Monte Cristo's, where a man dressed as an abbé walks past him into the inner rooms; the count explains it was his friend the Abbé Busoni, just arrived in Paris.

Danglars is gloomy: a Trieste banker, Jacopo Manfredi, has gone bankrupt owing him a million, on top of 700,000 francs lost in Spain, which he blames on his wife's 'dreams'. The count sorts fortunes into three classes and politely places Danglars' in the third, built on credit and easily shaken; six or seven months like this would ruin him. Danglars blusters. Talk turns to the Cavalcanti: the major has drawn 40,000 francs and opened an account of 5,000 a month for his son. The count calls the major a miser, guesses he came to find Andrea a wife, and remarks that such fathers may give millions if the son marries to their liking, perhaps a banker's daughter.

Danglars admits he would like Andrea for Eugénie, saying Albert would hardly care. He sneers that Madame de Morcerf's trip to the seaside will do her good, as it is the air she breathed in her youth, and that while he really is named Danglars, Morcerf is not: when Danglars was a clerk, Morcerf was a fisherman called Fernand Mondego. He hints at rumors from Greece. The count says he has heard the name Fernand Mondego in connection with Ali Pasha of Yanina (Ali Tepelini), and suggests Danglars ask his correspondent at Yanina what part a Frenchman of that name played in Ali's downfall. Danglars rushes off to write the letter.

title: The Office of the King’s Attorney
summary: Madame Danglars meets Villefort secretly in his office. He confesses he buried their newborn at Auteuil believing it dead, but a year later the box was gone. The child may have lived, and Monte Cristo seems to know their secret.
details: Veiled and changing cabs, Madame Danglars slips into the Palais de Justice and is led by a private passage to Villefort's office. He bolts the door and says bitterly that his place should be on the prisoner's bench, not the judge's seat. She speaks of the dinner, of the 'poor innocent offspring of mine, which I never even kissed', and of the bones the count found. Villefort tells her the truth is worse: nothing was found, because nothing was there.

He tells the story. She gave birth in the red damask room, and the baby seemed lifeless. He put it in a chest, buried it in the garden, and was stabbed by a Corsican who had sworn a vendetta (blood feud) against him. She helped him back to the house, a duel was given as the excuse for his wound, and while he spent months recovering, she, the widow of M. de Nargonne, married Danglars. A year later he cancelled the lease, returned at night and dug everywhere, but the chest had vanished. A corpse would have been taken to a magistrate, so he concluded the child might have been alive, and the Corsican might have saved it.

At the foundling hospital he learned that on that same night, 20 September, a baby had been left wrapped in half of a fine napkin marked with half a baron's crown and the letter H, the mark on all her linen. Six months later a woman claimed the child with the other half of the napkin. His agents traced her to Châlons, then lost her. Since Monte Cristo spoke of finding remains that could not have been there, Villefort is sure the count knows their secret. He asks whether she ever told anyone, kept a diary, or talks in her sleep, and vows to find out within a week who this Count of Monte Cristo really is.

title: A Summer Ball
summary: Albert returns from the seaside and invites Monte Cristo to his parents' summer ball, saying his mother especially wants him there. The count hints that Danglars also wants out of the engagement, then sends Bertuccio to Normandy after learning Madame Danglars visited the Palais.
details: Madame de Morcerf and Albert return from Tréport, and Albert hurries to see the count, who greets him with his usual cool reserve. Albert hears about the Auteuil dinner; the count stresses that young Cavalcanti only 'calls himself' a count. Albert declares that Eugénie would make a charming mistress but an awful wife, and that what he really wants is a wife like his mother, at which the count turns pale. Albert has even tried, by letter, to make Franz fall for Eugénie. Franz is returning soon, summoned by Villefort to marry Valentine.

The count tells Albert to relax: Danglars would pay double to break the engagement himself, since he is taken with someone else. Albert, a little stung, invites the count to his father's summer ball on Saturday and asks him to bring the Cavalcanti. The count refuses to present Andrea, saying he hardly knows him and was only recommended by 'a good abbé, who may be deceived'. He hesitates to come at all until Albert says his mother begs him to; she has talked of nothing else for four days. The Countess G— thinks he is Lord Ruthven (a famous fictional vampire), while Madame de Morcerf takes him for a Cagliostro, a mysterious magician. He accepts, and asks Albert to bring Franz to see him.

As Albert drives away, Bertuccio reports that 'she' went to the Palais and stayed an hour and a half before going straight home. The count tells him to go and find the little estate in Normandy they had discussed, and Bertuccio leaves that evening.

title: The Inquiry
summary: Villefort has the police look into Monte Cristo. The Abbé Busoni and Lord Wilmore give a supposed police agent harmless, contradictory accounts of 'M. Zaccone'. Lord Wilmore then turns out to be the count in disguise, and the 'agent' was Villefort himself.
details: Villefort writes to M. de Boville, the former prison inspector now high in the police. The reply says the count is an intimate friend of Lord Wilmore, a rich Englishman, and known to the Abbé Busoni, a Sicilian priest famed for his good works in the East. Further reports describe the abbé's austere little house near Saint-Sulpice and Wilmore's rented lodgings; Wilmore, oddly, never speaks a word of French.

A visitor claiming to come from the prefect of police calls on the abbé at night. Wearing a monk's cowl and huge spectacles, the abbé tilts his lamp so the light falls on his visitor's face while his own stays in shadow. He says the count's real name is Zaccone, son of a rich Maltese shipbuilder and his childhood playmate; he bought his title, has a modest income, served in the navy, may be a Lutheran, and was decorated by the pope for helping Christians in the East. His only enemy is Lord Wilmore. The count had never been to France before; six months ago he asked the abbé for advice, and the abbé recommended Bartolomeo Cavalcanti. The Auteuil house is to become a lunatic asylum. The abbé politely refuses the visitor's donation for the poor.

Lord Wilmore, red-whiskered and dressed in the fashion of 1811, speaks with more spite. He says Zaccone fought for an Indian prince against the English, was captured and escaped from the prison hulks by swimming, then fought in Greece and found a silver mine in Thessaly. He is in France for railways and a new telegraph system, and is digging up Auteuil looking for a mineral spring. Wilmore claims they have fought three duels over a seduced wife, and shows a fresh scar. When the visitor leaves, Wilmore pulls off his wig, whiskers, false jaw and scar, and becomes the Count of Monte Cristo. The 'agent' who returns home is M. de Villefort, who sleeps soundly for the first time since the dinner.

title: The Ball
summary: At the Morcerfs' ball, gossip spreads the police's version of Monte Cristo's past. Mercédès notices that the count refuses all food and drink under her husband's roof, and pointedly takes his arm to lead the guests into the garden.
details: On a hot July night the Morcerf garden glows with lanterns. Villefort has told Madame Danglars she must be seen at the ball, so she comes, dazzling. Eugénie and Valentine arrive arm in arm in white. Albert jokes that Madame Danglars is the seventeenth person to ask whether the count is coming; she reports that at the Opera he tossed a ring to the dancer Elssler. Madame de Villefort confides the 'secret' the police have just discovered: the count's family name is Zaccone, he is Maltese, served in India, owns a mine in Thessaly, and plans a water-cure at Auteuil. When Albert introduces Morrel, Madame de Villefort is cold to him, but across the room Valentine raises her bouquet of forget-me-nots to her lips.

Every eye turns as the count enters. He and Madame de Morcerf exchange only a silent bow. Albert amuses him with sharp portraits of pompous academicians and peers. Danglars joins them, and the count mentions that a Frankfurt bank has just failed; Danglars, pale, has already paid out 200,000 francs on their drafts and begs him not to mention it in front of young Cavalcanti.

Mercédès watches the count refuse every ice and drink, and asks Albert to press him; he still refuses. She tells her son the count has never been willing to eat under M. de Morcerf's roof, and concludes his abstinence is deliberate. Hearing he finds the room stifling, she has the blinds thrown open, then invites her husband's guests into the garden and asks the count for his arm. He almost staggers, and the look they exchange seems to her to last a century.

title: Bread and Salt
summary: Alone in the conservatory, Mercédès keeps offering Monte Cristo fruit, which he refuses, and questions him about his past. He speaks of a girl he once loved who married another. Then news arrives that the Marquis de Saint-Méran has died.
details: Mercédès leads the count to the greenhouse and offers him Muscatel grapes; he says he never eats them. She offers a peach; he refuses again. She reminds him of the Arab custom by which those who share bread and salt under one roof become friends forever. He replies that in France eternal friendships are as rare as that custom. When she asks, gripping his arm, whether they are friends, he goes deathly pale, then flushes, and answers, 'Certainly, we are friends; why should we not be?'

She asks if he has suffered; he has, deeply. Is he married? No: the young woman seen with him at the Opera is a slave he bought in Constantinople, a prince's daughter he has adopted, having no one else to love. He says that 'at Malta' he loved a young girl and was about to marry her when war carried him away; when he came back, she was married. He has forgiven her, and claims he does not hate those who separated them. When he refuses the grapes again, she flings them into the bushes: 'Inflexible man!'

Albert runs in with bad news. Villefort has come to fetch his wife and daughter: Madame de Saint-Méran has just reached Paris with word that the marquis died on the road from Marseilles, while coming to hurry on Valentine's marriage to Franz, and Valentine fainted. Albert makes a careless joke, and his mother joins his hand with the count's, asking again if they are friends. The count replies only that he is her most respectful servant, and she leaves in tears. Morrel leaves the ball soon after Valentine.

title: Madame de Saint-Méran
summary: The grieving Marquise de Saint-Méran arrives with news of her husband's sudden death. Feverish, she insists Valentine marry Franz at once, describes a white figure touching her glass in the night, and sends for a notary. Dr. d'Avrigny is called.
details: Alone in his study, Villefort goes over his secret list of enemies and decides none of them would have waited so long to strike. Perhaps, he thinks, the Corsican told the story to some priest, but what interest could Monte Cristo have in it? His mother-in-law bursts in: M. de Saint-Méran is dead. Unwell but determined to see Valentine, he took his usual lozenges on the road from Marseilles, fell into an unnaturally deep sleep, cried out and died. A doctor called it apoplexy (a stroke). She has had his body sent on to the family vault.

Villefort fetches his family from the ball. Valentine sits with her grandmother, who keeps a bottle of orangeade, her usual drink, by her bed, and then visits Noirtier, who comforts her with his eyes.

Next morning the marquise is feverish and insists on seeing Villefort. She wants the marriage to Franz, son of the royalist general killed before Napoleon's return, hurried on because she feels she has little time left; she reproaches Villefort for forgetting her daughter Renée. She says that in the night, with her eyes closed, she saw a white figure enter through the door from Madame de Villefort's dressing room and heard her glass being moved, and she believes it was her husband's spirit. She drinks a glass of orangeade and demands a notary. Valentine thinks of confessing her love for Maximilian, but knows her proud grandmother despises anyone not noble. While the notary is with the marquise, Valentine meets Dr. d'Avrigny, an old family friend, who finds the symptoms strange. She walks to the garden gate and hears Maximilian calling her.

title: The Promise
summary: Valentine promises to run away with Maximilian rather than sign her marriage contract, but on the chosen night her grandmother dies. Hiding in the garden, Maximilian overhears Dr. d'Avrigny tell Villefort she was poisoned. Noirtier then swears he will stop the marriage himself.
details: Maximilian tells Valentine that Franz has just arrived in Paris. She refuses to defy her father and her dying grandmother, and turns down his offer to take her to his sister's and marry her. He calmly announces he will kill himself the day she marries, and she gives in: if they force her to sign, she will come to him and they will flee. She swears it by her mother. Her letter arrives: the contract will be signed at nine that evening, so he should meet her at the gate at a quarter to nine.

That night he waits with ladders and a carriage, but Valentine never comes and the house stays dark. He climbs the wall and hides as Villefort and Dr. d'Avrigny walk into the garden. Madame de Saint-Méran is dead. The doctor says her convulsions looked like tetanus, but they are also the symptoms of vegetable poison, and he is convinced she died of brucine or strychnine. Villefort admits that only Valentine, her heir, gains by her death. The doctor wonders whether Barrois could have given her by mistake some of the brucine prescribed for Noirtier. Villefort begs him to avoid a scandal. D'Avrigny agrees to keep silent, but warns him to watch carefully, since the evil may not stop here.

Maximilian slips into the house and finds Valentine praying beside the body; Franz arrived just as her grandmother was dying. Morrel says he heard the news from servants, keeping the doctor's words to himself. Valentine leads him to Noirtier and declares she loves him. Noirtier rejects both of Morrel's plans, running away or provoking Franz to a duel: help will come from Noirtier himself, and the contract will not be signed. Morrel swears to wait for his decision and goes home.

title: The Villefort Family Vault
summary: The Marquis and Marquise de Saint-Méran are buried together at Père-Lachaise. Straight afterwards Villefort hurries Franz into signing the marriage contract, until Barrois announces that Noirtier demands to speak with Franz at once.
details: Two days later a double funeral takes place, the marquis's coffin having arrived from the south, and both are laid in the Villefort vault at Père-Lachaise cemetery beside their daughter Renée. In a mourning coach, Beauchamp, Debray, Château-Renaud and Albert discuss the sudden deaths; Beauchamp doubts that grief could cause a stroke in so slight a woman. They note that Valentine, and so Franz, will inherit a fortune, doubled when 'the old Jacobin' Noirtier dies. No one suspects the doctor's secret. At the cemetery Albert introduces Morrel to Franz, and Morrel, bound by his oath, bows politely, though it pains him to hear that Franz has seen Valentine.

Villefort takes Franz home and, citing the marquise's dying wish, proposes signing the contract that very day. Valentine will spend her three months of mourning on her new estate of Saint-Méran, where a quiet civil wedding can be held in a few days. Franz agrees and goes to fetch his witnesses, Albert and Château-Renaud. Valentine is stunned, and Madame de Villefort sits pale in the shadows, clutching Edward.

The notary first tells Franz that Noirtier has disinherited Valentine because of this marriage. The will is legally void, since Noirtier gave away more than the law allows, but Villefort says he will never challenge it while he lives. Franz answers nobly that he seeks happiness, not money. Villefort assures him Noirtier's mind is so weak that he has forgotten Franz's name. At that moment Barrois appears: M. Noirtier wishes to speak immediately to M. Franz de Quesnel, Baron d'Épinay, and if refused, he will have himself carried into the drawing room. Over Villefort's objections, Franz insists on going, and follows the joyful Valentine downstairs.

title: A Signed Statement
summary: Noirtier has Franz read a hidden document about his father's death in 1815: General d'Épinay was not murdered but killed in a fair duel after refusing to join a Bonapartist plot. Asked who killed him, Noirtier spells out the answer: himself.
details: Villefort whispers to Valentine that she is forbidden to understand anything that might delay the marriage. Through his eyes, Noirtier guides her to a key, an old writing desk, and a secret compartment that Barrois opens. Inside is a packet tied with black string, addressed to a General Durand, and Noirtier wants Franz to read it.

It is a report of a meeting of a Bonapartist club in the Rue Saint-Jacques on 5 February 1815, the night Franz's father disappeared. General de Quesnel had been recommended by a letter from Elba as loyal to Napoleon, despite being made a baron by Louis XVIII, and was brought blindfolded to the meeting. The letter spoke of Napoleon's return and promised more news on the arrival of the Pharaon, Morrel's ship. The general refused to join, declaring himself a royalist, and said that keeping their secret would make him an accomplice. Threatened, he swore an oath of silence. But in the carriage home he kept insulting them, so the club's president stopped at the Quai des Ormes and challenged him. By lantern light on icy steps, with a short sword hidden in his cane, the president fought him. The general fell twice and died; the witnesses threw his body into the river. The president had been wounded three times. The three witnesses signed the statement to prove it was an honorable duel, not murder.

Franz begs to know the president's name. Villefort insists it cannot be known, while Valentine, who has often seen two scars on her grandfather's right arm, draws back. Using the dictionary, Franz goes through the letter M until Noirtier stops him at 'myself'. 'You killed my father?' 'Yes.' Franz collapses into a chair, and Villefort flees the room, tempted to smother what life remains in the terrible old man.

title: Progress of Cavalcanti the Younger
summary: Andrea Cavalcanti, now accepted in Paris society, courts Eugénie with Danglars' encouragement while Albert looks on unbothered. Danglars asks Monte Cristo to press the Morcerfs for a decision, then receives news from Greece about 'Fernand and Yanina'.
details: The 'major' has gone back to the gaming tables of Lucca, leaving Andrea his papers. In two weeks Andrea has become a fashionable figure, called count and rumored to be heir to riches buried in the quarries of Saravezza. When Monte Cristo calls on the Danglars, the baroness, still nervous of him since Auteuil, is soon charmed again. Andrea sighs and gazes at Eugénie, who coldly escapes to her music room with her singing teacher Louise d'Armilly. Danglars sends Andrea in after them, and the count smiles to hear him sing a Corsican song, which reminds him of Benedetto.

Madame Danglars praises her husband's calm over a loss at Milan; the count notes that Danglars now hides his losses, and advises her to build a fortune of her own, which makes her blush. She tells him Franz broke off his engagement to Valentine yesterday, for unknown reasons, and that Villefort is taking it 'like a philosopher'. Danglars keeps calling Andrea 'Prince Cavalcanti'.

Albert arrives and hears that Eugénie is at the piano with Cavalcanti. He takes it with mocking good humor, which annoys Danglars. Aside, Danglars tells the count he will give his daughter only to a man who loves her, complains of 'obscurity' in the Morcerfs' past, teases the count about the proud Mercédès taking his arm at the ball, and asks him to make Albert's father either set a wedding date or break off. Called away, Danglars returns agitated: his courier from Greece has come, and there is 'a whole history connected with the names Fernand and Yanina'. He asks the count to take Albert away and send the father to him. The count turns aside to hide a look of pity, and leaves with Albert.

title: Haydée
summary: Monte Cristo introduces Albert to Haydée, who turns out to be the daughter of Ali Pasha of Yanina. She tells how her father was betrayed and killed, and how she and her mother were sold as slaves.
details: Driving home from the Danglars’ house, Albert complains that Andrea Cavalcanti is courting Eugénie Danglars and that the family is cold to him. The count says Danglars has asked him to push the Count of Morcerf, Albert’s father, to settle the marriage. At the count’s house Albert hears music from a guzla (a Balkan stringed instrument) and learns that the player is Haydée, a slave the count bought in Constantinople. She is also the daughter of Ali Tepelini, Pasha of Yanina, the ruler Albert’s father served when he made his fortune.

Albert begs to meet her. The count agrees on two conditions: Albert must tell no one, and he must never tell Haydée that his father served hers. Speaking Greek, which Albert cannot follow, the count tells Haydée to describe her father’s fate but to name neither the traitor nor the treason.

Speaking Italian, Haydée remembers her early childhood in Yanina. Then came a night flight to a kiosk (a pavilion) on the lake. There the loyal soldier Selim guarded a cavern full of gold and gunpowder. If Ali sent his dagger, Selim was to blow everything up. If Ali sent his ring, he was to put out the match. Ali had sent a trusted French officer to the sultan to negotiate. Soon a messenger arrived with the ring and news of a pardon. Selim put out the match and was stabbed at once by soldiers of Kourchid, the sultan’s commander, and Ali was killed in the fighting that followed. Twice Albert asks the French officer’s name, and twice Haydée says she cannot remember it.

Kourchid handed Haydée and her mother Vasiliki to the man who had done most to bring about Ali’s death. He sold them to slave merchants. Vasiliki dropped dead in Constantinople when she saw Ali’s head displayed over the city gate. Haydée was sold to an Armenian and later to the Sultan Mahmoud, and the count bought her from the sultan with an emerald. Albert leaves bewildered.

title: We hear From Yanina
summary: Franz breaks off his engagement to Valentine, and Noirtier makes her his heir. Danglars stalls Morcerf’s marriage proposal. Beauchamp’s newspaper reports that a French officer named Fernand betrayed Yanina, and Albert challenges Beauchamp to a duel.
details: After Noirtier’s revelation about Franz’s father, Franz writes to Villefort that the marriage is impossible. Madame de Villefort tells the waiting guests that Noirtier has had a fit. Valentine meets Maximilian at the garden gate and tells him “We are saved,” but she keeps the secret. Madame de Villefort then asks Noirtier to give his fortune back to Valentine. He agrees, and the next day he makes a new will leaving everything to Valentine, on condition that she never leaves him.

The Count of Morcerf puts on his general’s uniform and formally asks Danglars for Eugénie’s hand for Albert. Danglars coldly says he must think it over and refuses to explain. He hints at “calumnies” (slanders). Morcerf leaves in a fury, and Danglars notices that Morcerf never once asked whether the objection concerned him personally. That evening Andrea Cavalcanti is the last guest to leave Danglars’ house.

The next morning Danglars smiles over a paragraph in l’Impartial, Beauchamp’s newspaper, headed “We hear from Yanina.” It says the castle of Yanina was handed to the Turks by a French officer named Fernand. Albert finds Monte Cristo at a shooting gallery, where the count has shot ordinary playing cards full of holes so precisely that they look like other cards. Albert asks him to be his second. The count suggests asking Haydée what happened, then advises Albert to see Beauchamp alone. He refuses to act as second or to give lessons, and says Albert may learn why at some future time.

Beauchamp says he did not write the paragraph and that nobody else would connect “Fernand” with the Count of Morcerf. Albert’s threats make him refuse to retract without first looking into it. He asks for three weeks, until 21 September. Then he will either retract or fight.

title: The Lemonade
summary: Through Valentine, Noirtier tells Morrel they may marry once she comes of age. Then old Barrois drinks from Noirtier’s lemonade and dies in agony, and Dr. d’Avrigny proves that the lemonade was poisoned.
details: Noirtier sends for Maximilian, and Valentine interprets for him. Noirtier plans to move to separate lodgings and take Valentine with him. If Villefort refuses, she will wait ten months until she comes of age and has her own fortune. Then, with her grandfather’s consent, she will marry Maximilian. Until then they must be patient. Barrois, Noirtier’s old servant, is hot from running an errand, and Valentine offers him a glass of Noirtier’s lemonade.

Minutes later Barrois is seized by terrible convulsions. Morrel hides, and Villefort runs for Dr. d’Avrigny, who is upstairs with little Édouard. Madame de Villefort comes down slowly. She looks first at Noirtier and then at the dying servant, asks whether he has eaten, remarks that lemonade was bad for him, and leaves, saying she cannot bear the sight of blood. Morrel slips out by a back staircase.

D’Avrigny questions Barrois and Noirtier. Barrois made the lemonade but left it in the pantry, and Valentine carried it into the room. It was also Valentine who offered him a drink. Noirtier drank some too and noticed a bitter taste, but he feels just as he does after his usual Sunday dose of medicine. Barrois has a second, worse attack and dies.

Alone with Villefort, d’Avrigny says it is the same poison that killed Madame de Saint-Méran. He drips some lemonade into syrup of violets, which turns green. Barrois has been poisoned, he declares, and he will swear to it before God and man.

title: The Accusation
summary: D’Avrigny argues that the poison was meant for Noirtier and accuses Valentine of all the deaths. Villefort refuses to give up his daughter. The doctor withdraws from the house, and the frightened servants all leave.
details: D’Avrigny explains why Noirtier survived. For a year the doctor has been treating his paralysis with brucine, a poison in small doses, so his body is used to it. He traces a pattern behind the deaths. The Marquis and Marquise de Saint-Méran died, leaving a double fortune to inherit. Noirtier was spared while his will favored the poor, but as soon as he made a new will he was attacked. Look for whoever profits from the crime, he says.

It is Villefort who first speaks Valentine’s name. D’Avrigny presses on. She packed the Marquis’s medicines, prepared the Marquise’s drinks and carried in Noirtier’s lemonade. He denounces her to Villefort, as the king’s attorney, as the poisoner who deserves the scaffold.

Villefort falls to his knees. He will not hand his daughter to the executioner, and if she turned out to be innocent, he says, he would kill himself. D’Avrigny agrees to keep the secret but will never come to the house again. To the servants he announces that Barrois died of apoplexy (a stroke), and he quietly tells Villefort to throw away the syrup of violets.

That evening all the servants give notice, saying “death is in this house.” They praise their gentle young mistress Valentine as they go. Watching Valentine cry, Villefort glances at his wife and thinks he sees a faint, gloomy smile cross her lips.

title: The Room of the Retired Baker
summary: Andrea asks Danglars for Eugénie’s hand and is accepted. Caderousse demands more money from him. Andrea claims Monte Cristo is his real father, draws Caderousse a plan of the count’s house and tells him when it will be empty.
details: Andrea tells Danglars that his father has promised him 150,000 livres a year once he marries, and that his late mother left about two million. Danglars eagerly accepts him. Andrea lets slip a vulgar “Very good, father-in-law” that betrays his low birth. He says Monte Cristo refuses on principle to arrange marriages for anyone, and he gets Danglars to cash a draft signed by the count.

Caderousse refuses his monthly 200 francs and leaves a note summoning Andrea. Disguised in his groom’s livery, Andrea visits him on the Rue Ménilmontant, where Caderousse lives as “M. Pailletin, retired baker.” Over a Provençal breakfast Caderousse calls him “my little Benedetto” and brings up the past they shared “down there,” in the galleys (prison labor). He boasts that he once knew Danglars and the Count of Morcerf, and demands more money.

Andrea raises the allowance to 500 francs. Then he confides that he believes Monte Cristo is his true father. According to Andrea, the count pays “old Cavalcanti” to pose as his father and has made a will leaving him 500,000 francs. Caderousse is dazzled by talk of the count’s wealth. Andrea draws him a plan of No. 30 Champs-Élysées, showing the secretaire (a writing desk) in the dressing room, and mentions that the count will spend tomorrow night at Auteuil.

Caderousse also takes Andrea’s diamond ring. Andrea privately thinks Caderousse won’t sell it, “not at least till the day after tomorrow.” Alone, Caderousse studies the plan and mutters that whoever hurries Benedetto’s inheritance along will not be his worst friend.

title: The Burglary
summary: An anonymous letter warns Monte Cristo of a burglary, so he lies in wait and catches Caderousse in the act. Disguised as the Abbé Busoni, he makes Caderousse write a letter exposing Andrea, then lets him go, and an accomplice waiting outside stabs Caderousse.
details: At Auteuil, Bertuccio reports that the count’s house in Normandy is ready, a sloop (a small sailing ship) is waiting, and fresh horses are posted along the road to Tréport. Then Baptistin brings an anonymous letter. A man will break into the Paris house tonight to steal papers from the secretaire in the dressing room, and the count should deal with him personally, without the police. Suspecting assassins, the count sends all his servants to Auteuil and secretly returns to Paris with Ali. They wait in the dark bedroom, armed.

At a quarter to midnight a man cuts out a windowpane and climbs in, while a second man keeps watch in the street. When the burglar’s lantern lights his face, the count recognizes him. He puts a priest’s cassock and wig over the coat of mail he is wearing, steps in with a candle and greets the intruder: “Good-evening, my dear M. Caderousse.” Caderousse gasps, “The Abbé Busoni!”

Under questioning, Caderousse confesses everything. He escaped from the Toulon galleys with Benedetto, a young Corsican foundling, using a file supplied by an Englishman, Lord Wilmore. Benedetto now calls himself Andrea Cavalcanti, supposedly the count’s natural (illegitimate) son, and is about to marry Mademoiselle Danglars. When the abbé threatens to tell Danglars, Caderousse stabs him in the chest. The blade bends against the hidden mail, and the count wrenches his arm out of joint.

The count dictates a letter to Danglars: his daughter’s suitor is Benedetto, escaped convict No. 59. Caderousse signs it. He must leave by the window. If he gets home safely, the count promises to forgive him and pay him a small pension abroad. From the window the count watches the lookout run to the spot where Caderousse will climb down. As Caderousse reaches the ground, the man stabs him three times and runs, leaving him crying out for the reverend sir to help.

title: The Hand of God
summary: As he dies, Caderousse names Benedetto as his murderer and signs a statement. The count lectures him about God’s justice, then reveals who he really is, and Caderousse repents with his last breath.
details: The count sends Ali for the procureur du roi (the king’s prosecutor), M. de Villefort, and for a surgeon. Caderousse names his attacker: Benedetto. Benedetto gave him the plan of the house hoping that Caderousse would kill the count, making Benedetto his heir, or that the count would kill Caderousse and remove him. Drops from a phial (a small bottle) briefly revive the dying man. The count writes out a statement, “I die, murdered by the Corsican Benedetto, my comrade in the galleys at Toulon, No. 59,” and Caderousse signs it.

The count explains that Benedetto also sent the anonymous warning, and that he himself saw the ambush coming and chose not to warn Caderousse. Instead he left him to God’s judgment. He goes back over Caderousse’s life: betraying his friend while drunk, wasting the fortune the abbé once gave him, murdering the jeweller, the galleys, his rescue by the Englishman, and now this third crime. Caderousse screams that there is no God.

The count takes off his wig. Caderousse thinks he looks like the Englishman, Lord Wilmore. The count says he is neither Busoni nor Wilmore, swears by his father’s tomb, and whispers his real name. Terrified, Caderousse begs God’s pardon and dies. “One!” says the count over the body. When the surgeon and the procureur arrive, they find the Abbé Busoni praying beside the corpse.

title: Beauchamp
summary: The police fail to find Benedetto, and Andrea’s engagement to Eugénie goes ahead. Beauchamp returns from Yanina with proof that Albert’s father betrayed Ali Pasha, but he generously hands Albert the papers, and Albert burns them.
details: All Paris talks about the attempted robbery. The count says he was at Auteuil and that the Abbé Busoni happened to be staying in his house that night. Only Bertuccio turns pale whenever Benedetto’s name comes up. Villefort prepares the case, but after three weeks there is still no arrest. Meanwhile Andrea is received as Eugénie’s fiancé. Letters arrive from Major Cavalcanti approving the match, and it is agreed that Danglars will invest Andrea’s three million, although some people warn Andrea about the banker’s recent losses. Eugénie, who put up with Andrea only to get rid of Albert, now plainly dislikes him.

One morning Beauchamp appears at Albert’s house. He has spent the three weeks travelling to Yanina and back, and he shows his passport as proof. Sadly, he tells Albert that the newspaper paragraph was true. He hands over a statement signed by four leading citizens of Yanina: Colonel Fernand Mondego surrendered the castle for two million crowns. Beauchamp’s inquiries leave no doubt that this man is the Count of Morcerf. Albert collapses in tears.

Beauchamp says children cannot be blamed for their fathers’ faults, and he offers to destroy the only proofs. Albert burns every scrap and swears eternal friendship. But he is heartbroken about his father and terrified for his mother. Beauchamp warns him that it may not be over and asks pointedly about the broken Danglars engagement. To cheer Albert up, the two friends set off to visit Monte Cristo.

title: The Journey
summary: Monte Cristo whisks Albert away to his seaside house in Normandy. Three days later Beauchamp’s messenger brings a newspaper that openly names the Count of Morcerf as the traitor of Yanina, and Albert rushes back to Paris.
details: At the count’s house, Beauchamp says the matter is settled. The count is busy with papers about Cavalcanti that Danglars asked him to obtain. He insists he opposed the marriage and is forwarding the papers “like Pilate,” washing his hands of it. He mentions that Mademoiselle d’Armilly is going to Italy with letters of introduction from him. Complaining that the police keep sending him suspects in Caderousse’s murder, he invites Albert to the seaside. Albert accepts, and Beauchamp stays behind to watch the newspapers.

Albert says his mother Mercédès talks constantly about the count and calls him a noble nature, and the count sighs. They travel in the count’s carriage, with Ali driving relays of his black horses, and cover forty-eight leagues in eight hours. On the way the count remarks that he holds the power of life and death over Bertuccio.

The house near Tréport looks onto the sea, with a sloop in the creek flying the Monte Cristo arms. The friends spend three days hunting and fishing. On the third evening Albert’s valet Florentin gallops up with a letter and a newspaper from Beauchamp. Albert nearly faints. He borrows a horse and dashes off, leaving the paper behind. The count reads it. Another newspaper has printed that the French officer who surrendered Yanina and sold his benefactor to the Turks now calls himself the Count of Morcerf and sits among the peers.

title: The Trial
summary: Beauchamp tells Albert how his father was accused before the Chamber of Peers and defended himself well, until Haydée appeared with proof that he had betrayed Ali Pasha and sold her and her mother into slavery.
details: Beauchamp learned that the article came from a government newspaper, whose editor said a man from Yanina had brought in a stack of documents. In the Chamber of Peers (the upper house of parliament), the Count of Morcerf was disliked as an upstart. He knew nothing until a peer who was his enemy raised the matter. Morcerf went deathly pale, but he demanded an immediate inquiry. A committee of twelve met that same evening, and Beauchamp watched hidden in a gallery.

Morcerf spoke well. He produced letters from Ali Pasha and Ali’s ring, and claimed he was away negotiating for Ali when the pasha died. Ali had trusted him with Vasiliki and her daughter Haydée, he said, but they disappeared. The committee was almost won over when the president read a letter from a witness who claimed to have been present at Ali’s death.

A veiled woman entered. It was Haydée. She produced her birth and baptism records and a bill of sale from the slave merchant El-Kobbir. It recorded that a French colonel named Fernand Mondego had sold her and her mother for 400,000 francs, and that the Count of Monte Cristo later bought her for an emerald. Haydée told the committee that the count was in Normandy and knew nothing of what she was doing. She had always wanted to avenge her father.

Morcerf denied knowing her. Haydée cried out that he was the man who brought the false pardon, took the ring, stabbed Selim and sold them, and she told the peers to look at the scar on his right hand. He hid the hand, said he had no reply to make, and rushed from the room. The committee unanimously found him guilty of felony, treason and conduct unworthy of the House.

title: The Challenge
summary: Albert swears to kill whoever ruined his father. A clue leads him and Beauchamp to Danglars, who says it was Monte Cristo who advised him to write to Yanina, so Albert turns his anger on the count.
details: Beauchamp admires Haydée and suggests that whoever struck the blow was simply an agent of Providence. Albert wants an enemy of flesh and blood to fight. Beauchamp then reveals something he had kept back: the leading banker in Yanina told him that Danglars had written asking the same questions two weeks earlier.

At Danglars’ house they find Andrea Cavalcanti with the banker. Albert challenges Danglars and even offers to fight Andrea. Danglars calls him a mad dog. He admits writing to Yanina, saying a father has a duty to look into a suitor’s family. But he says it was Monte Cristo who suggested it, after Danglars remarked that Morcerf had made his fortune in Greece. The count saw the reply and knew Morcerf’s real name. Once the answer came, Danglars refused the marriage.

Albert puts the pieces together. The count bought Haydée, so he knew the truth. He advised Danglars to write, let Haydée tell her story in front of Albert, forbade Albert to mention his father’s name, and took Albert to Normandy just as the blow fell. Beauchamp agrees that Danglars was only a secondary player and that Albert must demand an explanation from Monte Cristo.

title: The Insult
summary: Mercédès begs Albert to stay friends with Monte Cristo, but he insults the count publicly at the Opera. The count accepts the challenge, swears he will kill Albert, and asks Maximilian and Emmanuel to be his seconds.
details: The count is home but sees no one, and he plans to go to the Opera, so Albert asks his friends to meet him there. He visits Mercédès, who is in bed with grief. He asks whether “M. de Morcerf” has enemies, and he reminds her that the count would eat nothing in their house, an Eastern sign of an enemy. Mercédès turns pale and begs him to keep the count’s friendship. Albert hints that she has special reasons for saying so. After he leaves, she sends a servant to follow him and gets dressed.

At the Opera, Albert, Beauchamp and Château-Renaud go to the count’s box, where Maximilian Morrel is sitting. Albert loudly demands an explanation. The count orders him out and remarks that showing off “is not becoming to everyone, M. de Morcerf,” a pointed reference to his father’s disgrace. Albert raises his glove to throw it, and Morrel catches his hand. The count takes the glove and promises to return it wrapped around a bullet.

The count tells Morrel that it was through Haydée that the Chamber learned of Morcerf’s treason, and that he will kill Albert before ten the next morning. When Morrel says Albert’s father loves him, the count flares up: “I will make him suffer.” Beauchamp comes to ask for an explanation, but the count refuses, though he lets Albert choose the weapons. They agree on pistols at eight in the Bois de Vincennes. Morrel and his brother-in-law Emmanuel agree to act as the count’s seconds.

title: The Night
summary: Mercédès comes secretly to Monte Cristo, calls him Edmond and begs for her son’s life. He shows her the letter that sent him to prison and tells her what he suffered. Then he promises Albert will live, which means letting Albert kill him instead.
details: The count is testing his pistols when a veiled woman rushes in. “Edmond, you will not kill my son!” It is Mercédès. She says she recognized him from his voice the moment she heard it. He replies coldly that his revenge has nothing to do with Ali Pasha. It is aimed at “the fisherman Fernand, the husband of Mercédès the Catalane.”

Mercédès blames herself for not waiting for him. He shows her the yellowed letter that Danglars wrote and Fernand posted, denouncing Edmond Dantès as a Bonapartist agent. The count took it from the prison file when he posed as a clerk of Thomson & French. He tells her of fourteen years in a dungeon of the Château d’If, so close to her, and of his father starving to death. Mercédès says she suffered too. For ten years she dreamed every night that he died being thrown from the Château d’If.

When she says she has seen the man she loved about to murder her son, the count breaks down and promises that Albert will live. But he cannot live with the public insult, so the duel will still take place, and it is his own blood that will be spilled. Mercédès trusts God, thanks him and tells him her heart has not changed. When she has gone he cries out that he was a fool not to tear his heart out on the day he resolved to take revenge.

title: The Meeting
summary: Expecting to die, Monte Cristo rewrites his will in favor of Maximilian and Haydée. But on the dueling ground Albert apologizes in front of everyone, saying the count was right to take revenge on his father.
details: The count grieves over his ruined plans. He adds a note to his will saying that his death is by his own choice, and that Morcerf, Danglars and Villefort should know their punishment is only delayed. He finds Haydée asleep outside his door and realizes that while Mercédès remembered her son, he forgot that he had a daughter. He leaves Maximilian twenty million francs hidden in his grotto on Monte Cristo, which Bertuccio knows how to find, and hopes Maximilian will marry Haydée. The rest, about sixty million, goes to Haydée. She wakes, reads the will and tears it up, saying that if he dies she will need nothing. Then she faints. For the first time he wonders whether she loves him as more than a daughter. He copies the will out again.

Morrel and Emmanuel arrive early. Morrel failed to get swords substituted for pistols, but he has won the count the first shot at twenty paces. The count shows them his skill by shooting away the four sides of an ace of clubs. Morrel begs him to spare Albert, and the count calmly replies that Albert will kill him. At the meeting place he asks whether Morrel’s heart is free. When Morrel says he loves a young girl, the count murmurs, “Poor Haydée!”

Albert has asked all his friends to attend, so Franz and Debray turn up too. Albert arrives late and pale. Before everyone, he says he blamed the count for exposing his father, but he has since learned the count had the right. That right came not from Ali Pasha’s betrayal but from the fisherman Fernand’s treachery toward the count and the misery it caused. Albert thanks him for not being harsher and offers his hand. The witnesses are stunned, and Château-Renaud and Debray are openly scornful.
